# React Native Worklets: Multithreading engine for your apps and libraries

---

# Memory

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/category/memory

# Memory

Copy values between runtimes or share state that more than one runtime needs to access.
Start with [Sharing memory](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/sharing-memory#choosing-between-them) to choose a memory primitive, or follow [Synchronizing data](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/synchronizing-data) for practical examples.

## Choose a memory primitive

* [`Serializable`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/serializable) — Transfer a value as an independent copy. Changes to the copy do not update the original.
* [`Synchronizable`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/synchronizable) — Keep shared state in native memory so multiple runtimes can read and write it.
* [`Shareable`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/shareable) — Keep a value on a host runtime and access it from guest runtimes.

## Create a value

* [`createSerializable`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/createSerializable) — Create an opaque reference to a serialized value. Scheduling APIs usually handle serialization for you.
* [`createSynchronizable`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/createSynchronizable) — Create a shared value in native memory.
* [`createShareable`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/createShareable) — Create a value hosted on a specific runtime.

## Inspect a value

* [`isSerializableRef`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/isSerializableRef) — Check whether a value is a Serializable reference.
* [`isSynchronizable`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/isSynchronizable) — Check whether a value is a Synchronizable.

## Customize serialization

* [`registerCustomSerializable`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/registerCustomSerializable) — Define how a custom type is transferred between runtimes.

## Deprecated APIs

These older APIs use different terminology. Follow their replacement guidance when updating existing code.

* [`makeShareable`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/makeShareable)
* [`makeShareableCloneRecursive`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/makeShareableCloneRecursive)
* [`makeShareableCloneOnUIRecursive`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/makeShareableCloneOnUIRecursive)

---

# Threading

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/category/threading

# Threading

Run work on another runtime, return a result, or create a worker for background calculations.
Start with [Running worklets on the UI runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/running-on-the-ui-runtime) to compare asynchronous and synchronous calls. See [Call tables](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/call-tables) for which runtimes can call each API.

## Run on the UI Runtime

* [`scheduleOnUI`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnUI) — Schedule work without waiting for a result.
* [`runOnUIAsync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnUIAsync) — Run work asynchronously and await its result.
* [`runOnUISync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnUISync) — Run work synchronously on the calling thread, blocking until the result is ready.
* [`UIRuntimeId`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/uiRuntimeId) — Identify the UI Runtime when an API takes a runtime ID.

## Run on a Worker Runtime

* [`createWorkletRuntime`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/createWorkletRuntime) — Create and configure a worker runtime.
* [`scheduleOnRuntime`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnRuntime) — Schedule work on a worker without waiting for a result.
* [`runOnRuntimeAsync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnRuntimeAsync) — Run work on a worker and await its result.
* [`runOnRuntimeSync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnRuntimeSync) — Access a worker runtime synchronously from the calling thread.

## Return to the RN Runtime

* [`scheduleOnRN`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnRN) — Schedule a function on the React Native runtime, for example to update React state.

## Address a runtime by ID

Use these variants when you have a runtime ID instead of a `WorkletRuntime` object.

* [`scheduleOnRuntimeWithId`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnRuntimeWithId) — Schedule work without waiting for a result.
* [`runOnRuntimeAsyncWithId`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnRuntimeAsyncWithId) — Run work asynchronously and await its result.
* [`runOnRuntimeSyncWithId`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnRuntimeSyncWithId) — Run work synchronously and return its result.

## Deprecated APIs

For new code, use the replacements linked from these reference pages.

* [`runOnUI`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnUI) — Use `scheduleOnUI`.
* [`runOnJS`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnJS) — Use `scheduleOnRN`.
* [`runOnRuntime`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnRuntime) — Use `scheduleOnRuntime`.
* [`executeOnUIRuntimeSync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/executeOnUIRuntimeSync) — Use `runOnUISync`.
* [`callMicrotasks`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/callMicrotasks) — Legacy helper for manually flushing UI microtasks.

---

# Utility

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/category/utility

# Utility

Inspect where your code is running and which Worklets features are available.
See [Runtime kinds](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds) for the difference between the RN, UI, and Worker Runtimes.

## Identify the runtime and thread

* [`getRuntimeKind`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/getRuntimeKind) — Get the kind of runtime executing the current code.
* [`getCurrentThreadId`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/getCurrentThreadId) — Get the platform-specific ID of the executing thread. A runtime and a thread are different things.

## Check the runtime kind

* [`isRNRuntime`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isRNRuntime) — Check whether code is running on the React Native runtime.
* [`isUIRuntime`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isUIRuntime) — Check whether code is running on the UI Runtime.
* [`isWorkerRuntime`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isWorkerRuntime) — Check whether code is running on a Worker Runtime.
* [`isWorkletRuntime`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isWorkletRuntime) — Check whether code is running on either a UI or Worker Runtime.

## Check functions and configuration

* [`isWorkletFunction`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isWorkletFunction) — Check whether a function has been workletized.
* [`isBundleModeEnabled`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isBundleModeEnabled) — Check whether Bundle Mode is enabled.

---

# Import forwarding

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode/importForwarding

# Import forwarding

Import forwarding is a feature of Bundle Mode that lets you use third-party
libraries inside worklet functions without adding boilerplate code.

To understand the motivation behind this feature, let's look at the ambiguity
of using imports inside worklet functions.

## Motivation

Say you have the following code:

```javascript
import { foo } from 'my-library';
import { scheduleOnUI } from 'react-native-worklets';

function worklet() {
  'worklet';
  foo();
}

scheduleOnUI(worklet);
```

Your intent is clearly to invoke `foo` from `my-library` inside the worklet function —
there shouldn't be any ambiguity. But consider another example.

Say `my-library` is a library that provides a counter:

```javascript title="my-library/index.js"
let value = 0;

export function incrementValue() {
  value++;
}

export function getValue() {
  return value;
}
```

And then you use it like this:

```javascript
import { incrementValue, getValue } from 'my-library';
import { scheduleOnUI } from 'react-native-worklets';

incrementValue();

function worklet() {
  'worklet';
  const value = getValue();
  console.log(value);
}

scheduleOnUI(worklet); // does it log 0 or 1?
```

Different JavaScript Runtimes don't share any state, so the invocation of
`incrementValue` on the RN Runtime didn't affect the `value` variable on the
Worklet Runtime.

So what's the intent behind the `getValue` invocation inside the worklet function here?
Did the author want to print the state of the RN Runtime or the Worklet Runtime?
Both interpretations are valid, but during static analysis of the code — which
the Worklets Babel plugin does — it's impossible to tell which one is correct.

## Disambiguating manually

You can write the same code explicitly, without ambiguity.

### Printing RN Runtime state

```javascript
import { incrementValue, getValue } from 'my-library';
import { scheduleOnUI } from 'react-native-worklets';

incrementValue();
const value = getValue();

function worklet() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(value);
}

scheduleOnUI(worklet); // logs 1
```

Here you explicitly assigned the result of `getValue` to a variable and passed
that variable as a closure of the worklet function. It's clear that you wanted to print
the state of the RN Runtime.

### Printing Worklet Runtime state

```javascript
import { incrementValue } from 'my-library';
import { scheduleOnUI } from 'react-native-worklets';

incrementValue();

function worklet() {
  'worklet';
  const { getValue } = require('my-library');
  const value = getValue();
  console.log(value);
}

scheduleOnUI(worklet); // logs 0
```

You used `require` to import `getValue` inside the worklet function. There's no doubt
that you wanted to print the state of the Worklet Runtime.

### The cost of explicit disambiguation

Writing your code exactly as in the previous example requires you to
re-specify all the imports in each worklet function, which adds a lot of boilerplate:

```javascript
function incrementOnce() {
  'worklet';
  const { getValue, incrementValue } = require('my-library');
  incrementValue();
  const value = getValue();
  console.log(value);
}

function incrementTwice() {
  'worklet';
  const { getValue, incrementValue } = require('my-library');
  incrementValue();
  incrementValue();
  const value = getValue();
  console.log(value);
}

// etc...
```

## Using import forwarding

Import forwarding lets you state which imports used inside worklet functions should be
forwarded into the worklet body automatically, so you can drop that boilerplate.

You can configure it via the
[`importForwarding`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/plugin-options#importforwarding)
option of the Worklets Babel plugin.

### Dropping boilerplate

You can rewrite the code from the [Printing Worklet Runtime
state](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode/importForwarding#printing-worklet-runtime-state) example without boilerplate. First,
configure the Worklets Babel plugin:

```javascript
/** @type {import('react-native-worklets/plugin').PluginOptions} */
const workletsPluginOptions = {
  // ...
  importForwarding: { moduleNames: ['my-library'] },
};
```

Then rewrite the code like this:

```javascript
import { incrementValue, getValue } from 'my-library';
import { scheduleOnUI } from 'react-native-worklets';

incrementValue();

function worklet() {
  'worklet';
  const value = getValue();
  console.log(value);
}

scheduleOnUI(worklet); // logs 0
```

This works because you explicitly stated all imports from `my-library` should
be forwarded into worklet functions — the Worklet Runtime gets its own copy of `my-library`'s
state.

### Explicit closure capture

What if you wanted to print the state of both the RN Runtime and the Worklet
Runtime? The same closure pattern still works:

```javascript
import { incrementValue, getValue } from 'my-library';
import { scheduleOnUI } from 'react-native-worklets';

incrementValue();

const value = getValue();

function printRN() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(value);
}

function printWorklet() {
  'worklet';
  const value = getValue();
  console.log(value);
}

scheduleOnUI(printRN); // logs 1
scheduleOnUI(printWorklet); // logs 0
```

To learn more about closures, see [this section](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/closures)
of the Worklets documentation.

---

# overview

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode

# Overview

Bundle Mode is a feature that gives worklet functions access to your whole JavaScript bundle - meaning that any code that's present in the bundle can be executed in any worklet function and on any runtime. This means that third party libraries can be used in worklet functions without the need to patch them. It's also a performance improvement as worklet functions' code can benefit from all the optimizations that pre-compiled bytecode offers.

**Bundle Mode will be the default way of using worklet functions in the future.**

Instructions on how to enable it can be found [here](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode/setup).

## Legacy Eval Mode

The former way of using worklet functions - where each worklet function is serialized as a string and evaluated individually on the Worklet Runtime - is referred to as **Legacy Eval Mode**. It's still the default mode of running worklet functions, but we strongly recommend switching to Bundle Mode.

---

# Setup

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode/setup

# Setup

To use `react-native-worklets`'s Bundle Mode feature, you need to make the following changes in your repository:

## Configure Worklets plugin

1. **Modify your Babel configuration**. [Worklets plugin](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/about) needs to know that it has to prepare your code for the Bundle Mode. This is also the source of truth for your app to know if the Bundle Mode is enabled. In your `babel.config.js` file, add the following:

Babel plugin

```javascript {2-5,13}
/** @type {import('react-native-worklets/plugin').PluginOptions} */
const workletsPluginOptions = {
  bundleMode: true,
  strictGlobal: true, // optional, but recommended
}

module.exports = {
  presets: [
    ... // don't add it here :)
  ],
  plugins: [
    ...
    ['react-native-worklets/plugin', workletsPluginOptions],
  ],
};
```

Oxc plugin

The Oxc plugin doesn't need any options. [`bundleMode`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/plugin-options#bundlemode) and [`strictGlobal`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/plugin-options#strictglobal) are always on.

```javascript {7}
module.exports = {
  presets: [
    ... // don't add it here :)
  ],
  plugins: [
    ...
    'react-native-worklets/plugin-oxc/babel',
  ],
};
```

## Configure Metro

2. **Modify your Metro configuration**. Metro needs to be configured to pre-load Bundle Mode entry points into your JavaScript bundle. In your `metro.config.js` file, apply the config required for the bundle mode. For example:

Expo

```javascript {3,10}
// Learn more https://docs.expo.io/guides/customizing-metro
const { getDefaultConfig } = require("expo/metro-config");
const { getBundleModeMetroConfig } = require("react-native-worklets/bundleMode");

/** @type {import('expo/metro-config').MetroConfig} */
let config = getDefaultConfig(__dirname);

// Your modifications to the config

config = getBundleModeMetroConfig(config);

module.exports = config;
```

React Native Community

```javascript {6,12-16}
const {
  getDefaultConfig,
  mergeConfig,
} = require('@react-native/metro-config');

const { bundleModeMetroConfig } = require('react-native-worklets/bundleMode');

const config = {
  // Your Metro config
};

module.exports = mergeConfig(
  getDefaultConfig(__dirname),
  bundleModeMetroConfig,
  config
);
```

`bundleModeMetroConfig` sets `serializer.polyfillModuleNames`. `mergeConfig` replaces this array, it does not concatenate it. If your Metro config sets `serializer.polyfillModuleNames` too, use `getBundleModeMetroConfig`, which appends to your list:

```javascript
const {
  getDefaultConfig,
  mergeConfig,
} = require('@react-native/metro-config');

const { getBundleModeMetroConfig } = require('react-native-worklets/bundleMode');

const config = {
  // Your Metro config
};

module.exports = getBundleModeMetroConfig(
  mergeConfig(getDefaultConfig(__dirname), config)
);
```

## Enable seamless Metro bundling

*This step is optional but highly recommended.*

If you run the app after just executing the above steps, you will see an error "Failed to get the SHA-1 for ...":

This is due to the fact that Bundle Mode isolates each worklet function in a separate module (file) on the fly and the Metro bundler doesn't index these isolated modules in time.

To fix this issue you can do one of the following:

1. Reload the app and Metro a couple of times until Metro picks up all the new modules. You will have to do it each time. Not recommended.
2. Patch `metro` package for it to synchronously index new modules created by Bundle Mode. This is the recommended approach. **This patch does not require building React Native from source**. You can find patching instructions in the [Worklets repository](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/tree/main/packages/react-native-worklets/bundleMode/patches).

This patch is a temporary workaround until necessary changes are merged into Metro.

## Enable fast refresh on Worklet Runtimes

*This step is optional but highly recommended.*

React Native's Fast Refresh (hot reload) feature doesn't apply to Worklet Runtimes out of the box. Therefore, when you change a worklet function's code you will see an error "\[Worklets] Unable to resolve worklet with hash ...".

This is due to the fact that the Fast Refresh update wasn't sent to the Worklet Runtime and it doesn't know that a new worklet function with the given hash exists.

To fix this issue you can do one of the following:

1. Reload the app on each worklet code change. This virtually defeats the purpose of Fast Refresh. Not recommended.
2. Patch `metro-runtime` package for it to send Fast Refresh updates to Worklet Runtimes. This is the recommended approach. **This patch does not require building React Native from source**. You can find patching instructions in the [Worklets repository](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/tree/main/packages/react-native-worklets/bundleMode/patches).

This patch is a temporary workaround until necessary changes are merged into Metro.

## Final steps

Make sure to clear your Metro bundler's cache to ensure that all the changes are applied correctly.

NPM

```bash
npm start -- --reset-cache
```

YARN

```bash
yarn start --reset-cache
```

And that's it! You can now happily enjoy the Bundle Mode! You can learn more about using the Bundle Mode [here](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode/usage).

## Reference

To see how the setup looks in a real project, you can check out the [Bundle Mode Showcase App](https://github.com/software-mansion-labs/Bundle-Mode-showcase-app) repository.

---

# Usage

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode/usage

# Usage

## Running third party libraries in Worklets

Third party libraries have to be on an allow-list to use them in worklets. This is because libraries can come with side-effects that would break a Worklet Runtime. For instance, a library that imports something from React Native can't be used on a Worklet Runtime. This would load a second instance of React Native and break your app.

To add a library to the allow-list you only need to set `importForwarding.moduleNames` in the Worklets Babel plugin options. It's an array of library names. For instance, if you want to use `my-library` on a Worklet Runtime.

```javascript
/** @type {import('react-native-worklets/plugin').PluginOptions} */
const workletsPluginOptions = {
  bundleMode: true,
  strictGlobal: true, // optional, but recommended
  // highlight-next-line
  importForwarding: { moduleNames: ['my-library'] },
};
```

The `importForwarding` API is temporary and will be replaced with a more robust solution in the future.

## Running network requests in Worklets

In Bundle Mode, Worklet Runtimes come with a standalone networking module, no longer needing a feature flag. It's installed on every Worklet Runtime unless you opt out with [`enableNetworking: false`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/createWorkletRuntime#enablenetworking).

```tsx
const runtime = createWorkletRuntime({ name: 'worker' });

scheduleOnRuntime(runtime, async () => {
  'worklet';
  const response = await fetch('https://swmansion.com');
  console.log(response.status);
});
```

| API                                       | Supported                                             |
| ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| `fetch`, `Headers`, `Request`, `Response` | ✅                                                     |
| `XMLHttpRequest`                          | ✅                                                     |
| `Blob`, `FileReader`                      | ✅                                                     |
| `AbortController`, `AbortSignal`          | ✅                                                     |
| `FormData`                                | String fields only, encoded as `multipart/form-data`. |
| Response streaming                        | ❌                                                     |
| `WebSocket`                               | coming soon                                           |

Requests are made by the platform's own networking stack, they share the app's cookie storage and its TLS configuration.

## Reference

To see how the setup looks in a real project, you can check out the [Bundle Mode Showcase App](https://github.com/software-mansion-labs/Bundle-Mode-showcase-app) repository.

---

# Understanding closures

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/closures

# Understanding closures

## What are closures in worklet functions?

What makes [worklet functions](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/concurrency-model#worklet-functions) special is their **ability to capture variables from their surrounding scope**, similar to regular JavaScript functions. This feature is known as *closures*.

While a closure is [defined as both the function and its lexical environment](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Closures), here we will refer to closures as just the captured variables from the surrounding [scope](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Scope).

```tsx
const a = 1;
const b = 2;
const c = 3;

function addAB() {
  'worklet';
  return a + b + c;
  // You can access `a` and `b` and `c` here
  // because they are captured from the surrounding scope.

  // We will refer to `a`, `b`, and `c` as the closure of this worklet.
}
```

However, there are some important differences in how closures work in worklet functions compared to regular JavaScript functions.

## Closure behavior on the same JavaScript Runtime

If you call a worklet function on the same runtime where it's defined (the [React Native Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#rn-runtime)), its closure gets copies of references to the original variables. This means that reassigning the original variable will not affect the value inside the worklet function.

```tsx
let count = 0;

function logCount() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(count); // Always prints 0, even if `count` changes later.
}

count = 1;
logCount(); // prints 0
```

This works both ways, so if you reassign inside a worklet function, it won't affect the original variable in the surrounding scope.

```tsx
let count = 0;

function increment() {
  'worklet';
  count += 1; // This modifies the copy of `count`, not the original.
}

increment();
console.log(count); // Still prints 0
```

The behavior is slightly different for object (non-primitive) references:

* Reassigning the reference in the surrounding scope does not affect the worklet function's closure.

  ```tsx
  let obj = { value: 0 };

  function logValue() {
    'worklet';
    console.log(obj.value);
  }

  obj = { value: 1 };
  logValue(); // Prints 0
  ```

* Mutating the object inside the worklet function affects the object in the surrounding scope, since they reference the same object.

  ```tsx
  let obj = { value: 0 };

  function mutate() {
    'worklet';
    obj.value += 1;
  }

  mutate();
  console.log(obj.value); // Prints 1
  ```

* Mutating the object in the surrounding scope affects the object inside the worklet function, since they reference the same object.

  ```tsx
  let obj = { value: 0 };

  function logValue() {
    'worklet';
    console.log(obj.value);
  }

  obj.value = 1;
  logValue(); // Prints 1
  ```

## Closure behavior across different JavaScript Runtimes

When a worklet function is executed in a different JavaScript runtime than the Runtime of its origin (a [Worklet Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#worklet-runtime)), the closure behavior is different again. **The closure in the worklet function becomes an exact copy of the variables from the surrounding scope at the moment of its invocation.** This is a necessity due to the fact that different runtimes cannot share references to the same objects, they cannot share memory directly.

```tsx
let obj = { value: 0 };

function logValue() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(obj.value);
}

obj.value = 1;
runOnUISync(logValue); // Prints 0
```

## Global scoping

In the previous examples we used `console` inside worklet functions. Where does it come from?

In JavaScript, when you use a variable (an [identifier](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Identifier)) which isn't defined in the local [scope](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Scope) (i.e. inside the function), the JavaScript engine looks for it in the outer scopes, eventually reaching the [global scope](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Global_scope). The key point here is that each Worklet Runtime has its own, distinct global scope. This means that global variables are not shared between different runtimes.

**The accessed `console` object inside a worklet function is different on each Runtime!** It's available on every runtime because each Worklet Runtime defines its own `console` object in its global scope.

When you use a global variable inside a worklet function, and invoke it on a runtime - it will access the global scope of that runtime, not the global scope of the original JavaScript Runtime. If the variable doesn't exist in the target runtime's global scope, it will be `undefined`.

```js
import { runOnUISync } from 'react-native-worklets';

(globalThis.someValue = 42);

function logSomeValue(label) {
  'worklet';
  console.log(label, globalThis.someValue);
}

logSomeValue('RN global:'); // RN global: 42
// The UI Runtime has its own global scope.
runOnUISync(logSomeValue, 'UI global:'); // UI global: undefined
```

Step through the example and watch **Globals** in each runtime. `someValue` appears on RN, while UI has no value for it. The same function reads `42` on RN and `undefined` on UI because it accesses the global scope of the runtime it runs in.

To have access to a (copy of a) global variable inside a worklet function on a different runtime, you must explicitly assign it to the `globalThis` object on the target runtime. This can be done with a local reference in the closure:

```js
import { runOnUISync } from 'react-native-worklets';

(globalThis.someValue = 42);
const localSomeValue = globalThis.someValue;

function assignGlobal() {
  'worklet';
  (globalThis.someValue = localSomeValue);
}

function logSomeValue(label) {
  'worklet';
  console.log(label, globalThis.someValue);
}

runOnUISync(logSomeValue, 'UI global before:'); // undefined
runOnUISync(assignGlobal);
runOnUISync(logSomeValue, 'UI global after:'); // 42
```

Here, `localSomeValue` is captured by `assignGlobal`. UI still reads `undefined` before the assignment. After the assignment, its own **Globals** panel contains `someValue: 42`, and the next read returns `42`. The two runtimes still have separate global scopes.

---

# Runtime kinds

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds

# Runtime kinds

The Worklets library differentiates between two types of runtimes - **React Native Runtime** and **Worklet Runtimes**. **Worklet Runtimes** are further divided into **UI Runtime** and **Worker Runtimes**.

## RN Runtime

React Native Runtime - a JavaScript Runtime spawned by React Native. It's the Runtime where React lives and your app's JavaScript code is executed. This Runtime is executed by the React Native's [JS Thread](https://reactnative.dev/architecture/threading-model). This is the only Runtime that has access to the React Native APIs and the app's state and components.

You can learn more about it by reading the [JavaScript Runtime](https://reactnative.dev/docs/javascript-environment) article in the official React Native docs.

There's only one React Native Runtime in your app.

## Worklet Runtime

A JavaScript Runtime spawned by the Worklets library. It's pre-configured to be able to execute worklet functions. It doesn't share any memory with the React Native Runtime or other Worklet Runtimes, but it can communicate with them using specific APIs. It isn't coupled to any thread, but there might be a thread dedicated to its execution.

We differentiate between two kinds of Worklet Runtimes, **UI Runtime** and **Worker Runtimes**.

Each Worklet Runtime has a unique `runtimeId` that can be used to refer to it when communicating between runtimes or creating [Shareables](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/shareable) on a specific Worklet Runtime.

### UI Runtime

Special kind of a Worklet Runtime. Its primary role is to execute worklet functions which represent high-priority JavaScript tasks. The UI Runtime is mostly executed by the UI (main) thread. Examples of such tasks are:

* **Synchronous handling of native events**.\
  Responding to native events like touches on the UI thread allows to react to them on the same frame of the user interaction, without any perceivable delays.

* **Animation calculations**.\
  Running animations on a main thread, decoupled from heavy business logic on RN Runtime, ensures that they run without interruptions, maintaining stable frame rates.

UI Runtime can be periodically acquired by other threads (other runtimes) to synchronize data.

There's only one UI Runtime in your app.

### Worker Runtime

A Worklet Runtime spawned by [createWorkletRuntime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/createWorkletRuntime) API per user request. Worker Runtimes are designed to execute worklet functions in a separate thread. They allow for custom parallelization of JavaScript code execution, which can be useful for heavy computations or tasks that don't require immediate interaction with the user interface, like data processing or background tasks.

You can customize its behavior and the thread it runs on.

There can be multiple Worker Runtimes in your app running at the same time.

```js
import {
  getRuntimeKind,
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnUI,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function checkUI() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(getRuntimeKind()); // 2 (UI Runtime)
}

function checkWorker() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(getRuntimeKind()); // 3 (Worker Runtime)
}

console.log(getRuntimeKind()); // 1 (RN Runtime)
scheduleOnUI(checkUI);
const workerRuntime = createWorkletRuntime({ name: 'background' });
scheduleOnRuntime(workerRuntime, checkWorker);
```

---

# Sharing memory

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/sharing-memory

# Sharing memory

The Worklets library lets you run JavaScript on more than one thread. The moment you do that, you have to answer a question that
single-threaded JavaScript has always let you ignore: **how do two pieces of code, running at the same time, look at the
same data?**

This page explains why that question has no cheap answer in JavaScript, and why the Worklets library exposes three distinct shared
memory primitives — the [Serializable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/serializable), the [Synchronizable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/synchronizable),
and the [Shareable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/shareable) — instead of one.

## JavaScript is single-threaded on purpose

JavaScript is designed around a single-threaded execution model. One call stack, one event loop, one piece of code
running at a time, all neatly packed into **an abstraction called the JavaScript Virtual Machine — JSVM, which we'll call
a "Runtime" from here on**. That choice is load-bearing: it means a function that reads and mutates a variable
cannot be interrupted halfway through by another function doing the same thing. There are no data races, no torn reads,
no half-written objects. You never need a mutex to increment a counter.

The language leans on this guarantee everywhere. Closures capture variables by reference and expect those references to
stay coherent. Objects are mutable, passed by reference, and shared freely across the program. None of this would be
safe if two threads could touch the same heap at the same time — but in single-threaded JavaScript, it is safe by
construction.

## Parallelism and memory

So what exactly happens when we add another thread into the equation? The naive approach: just tell two threads to do
some work on the same Runtime. They might work for a short while, but very soon we'll hit an EXC\_BAD\_ACCESS exception —
at some point one thread is bound to change some underlying reference that the other thread assumes is stable.

The only thing we can do at this point is to give each thread its own Runtime. The crashes go away, everything runs in
parallel, but we have a new problem: the two Runtimes are like two separate worlds.

For example, you can't just "hand" a JavaScript object from one Runtime to another. A JavaScript object is a collection
of pointers into one specific engine's heap. Its prototype chain, its hidden class, its property storage or even the
garbage collector or the global object — all of it is engine-internal state that another Runtime has no way to
interpret. Force-interpreting such a collection of pointers in another Runtime would be like trying to read a pointer from one
process and dereference it in another process — it just doesn't work. At this point, probably the simplest way of
communicating and sharing data between these Runtimes is to connect via a WebSocket — but again, that's very naive.

How, then, do we share this data the right way — with the least overhead, in RAM, and preferably without unnecessary
copies? It depends on the context and the kind of data we want to share.

## Kinds of shared memory

We can categorize shared memory into three types, based on how they are implemented and how they behave across Runtimes:

### Copy-only memory — Serializable

The simplest of them all: a way to move any value from Runtime A to Runtime B as-is — a number, an object, a string,
essentially any value that can be expressed as data. However, changes to such a value on any Runtime aren't visible in
the other Runtimes. Each Runtime is unaware that it has a copy and simply treats its value as the original. **This is
the [Serializable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/serializable) primitive.**

Each to-be-copied value is serialized into a byte stream and sent through C++ to the other Runtime, where it's
reconstructed. This is straightforward for primitives like numbers and strings, but for objects it can be more
complex — for example, how do you handle an object that contains a circular reference? Or a function? The implementation
of the Serializable has to cover all these edge cases and at least produce a meaningful error when a value can't be
serialized.

![Serializable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/img/model-serializable.svg)

High-level overview of the Serializable memory model — no Runtime holds ownership of the value, they just exchange
copies of it.

From the user's perspective, a Serializable is an opaque C++ value that the Worklets library knows how to pass around and turn into
regular JavaScript values on the other side. In all cases, this is done implicitly by the library APIs, and you never
need to create Serializables directly.

### Unbound memory — Synchronizable

The simpler type of memory that is actually shared — meaning that changes to it on Runtime A will be seen by Runtime B
and all the other Runtimes — but not tied to any particular Runtime, *unbound*. This is achieved by keeping the actual
"real" value outside of any Runtime, in C++, guarded by mutexes and other synchronization primitives. Each JavaScript
Runtime holds just a specific kind of reference to the C++ value. Each read or write means crossing the boundary between
JavaScript and C++. Because the memory is thread-safe, each Runtime can safely access it at its own discretion. **This
is the [Synchronizable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/synchronizable) primitive.**

![Synchronizable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/img/model-synchronizable.svg)

High-level overview of the Synchronizable memory model — the value is kept outside of any Runtime, and each Runtime
holds a reference to it.

While it might seem like an ideal solution, the cost of keeping the value outside of a Runtime is significant. Each
access to the Synchronizable means a round trip through C++ and conversions — because our Runtime can't just use the
C++ type directly, the value has to be converted (to a Serializable) before it can be used in JavaScript. You're also
severely limited in what you can do with the value — you can't store anything Runtime-specific in it, like a function or
an object with a prototype chain, because it wouldn't make sense in another Runtime.

### Bound memory — Shareable

This more complex type of shared memory overcomes some issues of unbound memory, but at the cost of being *asymmetric and
bound to a particular Runtime*.

Operations on unbound memory are much more expensive than operations on plain JavaScript values, because each access has
to cross the boundary between JavaScript and C++ via JSI. Runtime-bound memory optimizes access time on a single
designated JavaScript Runtime, called the Host Runtime, by simply holding the value there as a plain JavaScript value.
Other Runtimes, called Guest Runtimes, only have a specific kind of reference that "knows" that the actual value lives
on another Runtime — if you want to access it with that reference, you must go to C++, lock the Host Runtime
exclusively, read the actual value, and return it to the Guest Runtime that initiated the read. **This is the
[Shareable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/shareable) primitive.**

![Shareable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/img/model-shareable.svg)

High-level overview of the Shareable memory model — the value is kept on the Host Runtime, and the Guest Runtimes hold
a reference to it.

**The Shareable should be the preferred way of handling non-trivial data sharing since it comes with the least overhead
when used correctly**. However, it requires a more careful design of your data flow and access patterns, to avoid too many
round trips between the Guest Runtimes and the Host Runtime.

## Compare the same update

Each example starts with a counter at `0`, increments it on the UI Runtime, and then reads it on the RN Runtime. The callback runs after the update, so the different results come from the memory primitive, not the order of execution.

Serializable

UI increments its own copy to `1`. RN still reads `0` from the original object. Passing a regular object would serialize it automatically; this example creates the reference explicitly to show the copy.

```js
import {
  createSerializable,
  scheduleOnRN,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

(globalThis.counter = { value: 0 });
const reference = createSerializable(globalThis.counter);

function readOnRN() {
  console.log('RN:', globalThis.counter.value); // 0
}

function incrementOnUI(counter) {
  'worklet';
  (globalThis.counter = counter);
  (globalThis.counter.value += 1);
  console.log('UI:', globalThis.counter.value); // 1
  scheduleOnRN(readOnRN);
}

scheduleOnUI(incrementOnUI, reference);
```

Synchronizable

UI updates the shared value to `1`, and RN reads `1` from the same Synchronizable. Each access goes through the shared memory outside both runtimes.

```js
import {
  createSynchronizable,
  scheduleOnRN,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

const counter = createSynchronizable(0);

function readOnRN() {
  console.log('RN:', counter.getBlocking()); // 1
}

function incrementOnUI() {
  'worklet';
  counter.setBlocking((value) => value + 1);
  console.log('UI:', counter.getBlocking()); // 1
  scheduleOnRN(readOnRN);
}

scheduleOnUI(incrementOnUI);
```

Shareable

UI owns the value and updates it directly to `1`. RN also reads `1`, but its `getSync` call must acquire the UI Runtime to read the hosted value.

```js
import {
  createShareable,
  scheduleOnRN,
  scheduleOnUI,
  UIRuntimeId,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

const counter = createShareable(UIRuntimeId, 0);

function readOnRN() {
  const value = counter.getSync();
  console.log('RN:', value); // 1
}

function incrementOnUI() {
  'worklet';
  (counter.value += 1);
  console.log('UI:', counter.value); // 1
  scheduleOnRN(readOnRN);
}

scheduleOnUI(incrementOnUI);
```

## Choosing between them

Each of these primitives has its own use cases, and the right one to use depends on your specific needs. Here are some
general guidelines:

* **You are passing a value across Runtimes once, and the other side does not need to observe further changes.** For
  example, you want to pass a configuration object between Runtimes.
  * Use a Serializable. Copy, pass and forget.
* **You need a value that multiple Runtimes read and write with similar frequency, and you need them to see each other's
  updates.** For example, you want to keep your application state in a single place and have all Runtimes be able to
  synchronize on it.
  * Use a Synchronizable. Read and write only when you need to, maybe even add an event-emitting layer on top of it to
    avoid polling.
* **One Runtime dominates access to the value, and other Runtimes only reach in occasionally.** For example, you have an
  animation engine that reads an animation state on every frame during a critical phase of the rendering pipeline, but
  sometimes you want to change that state based on user input. Basically, you're writing Reanimated.
  * Use a Shareable. Keep the value on the Host Runtime and let the Guest Runtimes read it when they need to, but limit
    the amount of reads and writes of the Guest to avoid too many round trips. Cache the value on the Guest Runtimes if
    you allow for eventual consistency.

The rest of this section documents each primitive in detail, along with the APIs —
[createSerializable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/createSerializable), [createSynchronizable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/createSynchronizable),
[createShareable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/createShareable) — for producing them.

---

# About

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/

# About

React Native Worklets is a library that runs JavaScript code on more than one thread in a React
Native app.

By default, React Native executes all of your JavaScript on one thread, the JS thread, in one
JavaScript runtime. Rendering, layout, touch handling, network callbacks and your business logic all
wait in the same queue. A long task on the JS thread delays everything that comes after it, and the
app stops responding until the task ends.

Worklets adds more JavaScript runtimes to your app:

* The **UI Runtime** runs on the UI (main) thread. Code on it can respond to every frame and every
  touch without waiting for the JS thread.
* **Worker Runtimes** run on their own background threads. You create them for work that must not
  block either the JS thread or the UI thread.

Each runtime has its own JavaScript heap, so runtimes do not share JavaScript objects. A
[worklet function](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/concurrency-model#worklet-functions) is a function that the
[Worklets plugin](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/about) prepares at build time, so that you can copy it to
another runtime and run it there. To move data between runtimes, Worklets gives you
[Serializables](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/serializable), [Shareables](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/shareable) and
[Synchronizables](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/synchronizable).

The example below runs the same app in two ways: with all of its work on the JS thread, and with
the work distributed across runtimes. Use the **Enable Worklets** switch to compare them:

Without Worklets

```js
import {
  applyEqualizer,
  applyTheme,
  decodeAudio,
  fetchFromBackend,
  layoutBlocks,
  mixChannels,
  parseMarkdown,
  playAudio,
  renderHtml,
  resolveLinks,
} from './mocks';

function refreshFeed(page) {
  const posts = fetchFromBackend(`/feed?page=${page}`);
  setNativeProps('feed', { posts: posts.items });
  console.log(`feed page ${page} ready`);
  setTimeout(() => refreshFeed(page + 1), 8);
}

function animateSpinner(angle) {
  setNativeProps('spinner', { rotation: angle });
  console.log(`spinner at ${angle}deg`);
  requestAnimationFrame(() => animateSpinner(angle + 16));
}

function streamAudio(chunk) {
  const buffer = decodeAudio(chunk);
  const equalized = applyEqualizer(buffer);
  const mixed = mixChannels(equalized);
  setNativeProps('speaker', { pulse: playAudio(mixed) });
  console.log(`chunk ${chunk} played`);
  setTimeout(() => streamAudio(chunk + 1), 32);
}

function renderMarkdown(doc, revision) {
  const ast = parseMarkdown(doc, revision);
  const linked = resolveLinks(ast);
  const blocks = layoutBlocks(linked);
  const styled = applyTheme(blocks);
  setNativeProps('article', renderHtml(styled));
  console.log(`rendered ${doc} r${revision}`);
  setTimeout(() => renderMarkdown(doc, revision + 1), 16);
}

function onPress(count) {
  console.log(`press #${count}`);
  renderUI(count);
}

streamAudio(1);
renderMarkdown('README.md', 1);
animateSpinner(0);
refreshFeed(1);
```

With Worklets

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';
import {
  applyEqualizer,
  applyTheme,
  decodeAudio,
  fetchFromBackend,
  layoutBlocks,
  mixChannels,
  parseMarkdown,
  playAudio,
  renderHtml,
  resolveLinks,
} from './mocks';

function refreshFeed(page) {
  const posts = fetchFromBackend(`/feed?page=${page}`);
  setNativeProps('feed', { posts: posts.items });
  console.log(`feed page ${page} ready`);
  setTimeout(() => refreshFeed(page + 1), 8);
}

function animateSpinner(angle) {
  setNativeProps('spinner', { rotation: angle });
  console.log(`spinner at ${angle}deg`);
  requestAnimationFrame(() => animateSpinner(angle + 16));
}

function streamAudio(chunk) {
  const buffer = decodeAudio(chunk);
  const equalized = applyEqualizer(buffer);
  const mixed = mixChannels(equalized);
  setNativeProps('speaker', { pulse: playAudio(mixed) });
  console.log(`chunk ${chunk} played`);
  setTimeout(() => streamAudio(chunk + 1), 24);
}

function renderMarkdown(doc, revision) {
  const ast = parseMarkdown(doc, revision);
  const linked = resolveLinks(ast);
  const blocks = layoutBlocks(linked);
  const styled = applyTheme(blocks);
  setNativeProps('article', renderHtml(styled));
  console.log(`rendered ${doc} r${revision}`);
  setTimeout(() => renderMarkdown(doc, revision + 1), 16);
}

function onPress(count) {
  console.log(`press #${count}`);
  renderUI(count);
}

const audio = createWorkletRuntime({ name: 'audio' });
const md = createWorkletRuntime({ name: 'markdown' });
scheduleOnRuntime(audio, streamAudio, 1);
scheduleOnRuntime(md, renderMarkdown, 'README.md', 1);
scheduleOnUI(animateSpinner, 0);
refreshFeed(1);
```

# Installation

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/getting-started/installation

# Installation

Check the [compatibility table](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/compatibility) to find the Worklets version that supports your React Native version.

## Step 1: Install the package

Install `react-native-worklets` package from npm:

NPM

```bash
npm install react-native-worklets
```

YARN

```bash
yarn add react-native-worklets
```

## Step 2: Configure your project

The remaining steps depend on how you build your app — pick your framework:

Expo

Run prebuild to update the native code in the `ios` and `android` directories.

NPM

```bash
npx expo prebuild
```

YARN

```bash
yarn expo prebuild
```

And that's it! The Worklets library is now configured in your Expo project.

Don't I need the Worklets babel plugin?

Since [Expo SDK 54](https://expo.dev/changelog/sdk-54-beta#notable-breaking-changes), the Expo starter template includes the Worklets babel plugin by default, so there's nothing to add. On older SDKs, add `react-native-worklets/plugin` to your `babel.config.js` as described in the React Native Community CLI tab.

To learn more about the plugin go to [Worklets plugin](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/about) section.

### Clear Metro bundler cache (recommended)

NPM

```bash
npx expo start --clear
```

YARN

```bash
yarn expo start --clear
```

React Native Community CLI

When using [React Native Community CLI](https://github.com/react-native-community/cli), you need to manually add the `react-native-worklets/plugin` plugin to your `babel.config.js`.

```js {7}
module.exports = {
  presets: [
    ... // don't add it here :)
  ],
  plugins: [
    ...
    'react-native-worklets/plugin',
  ],
};
```

Worklets Babel plugin comes with several options, you can explore what they are and how to use them in the [Options for Worklets Babel Plugin](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/plugin-options) section.

Why do I need this?

In short, the Worklets babel plugin automatically converts special JavaScript functions (called [worklet functions](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/concurrency-model#worklet-functions)) to allow them to be passed and run on the [Worklet Runtimes](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#worklet-runtime)

To learn more about the plugin go to [Worklets plugin](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/about) section.

### iOS

While developing for iOS, make sure to install [pods](https://cocoapods.org/) first before running the app:

```bash
cd ios && pod install && cd ..
```

### Clear Metro bundler cache (recommended)

NPM

```bash
npm start -- --reset-cache
```

YARN

```bash
yarn start --reset-cache
```

# Call tables

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/call-tables

# Call tables

Call tables are quick references that show **where a given scheduling function can be called from**, depending on whether [Bundle Mode](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode) is enabled or not.

### Why does Bundle Mode matter?

In [Legacy Eval Mode](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode#legacy-eval-mode), Worklet Runtimes only have a subset of functionalities of the RN Runtime, due to limitations of serialization of worklet functions. With Bundle Mode enabled, every runtime has access to the full JavaScript bundle, so most threading APIs become available on all runtimes.

### How to read a call table

Take [scheduleOnUI](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnUI) as an example:

| Mode             | RN Runtime | UI Runtime    | Worker Runtime |
| ---------------- | ---------- | ------------- | -------------- |
| Bundle Mode      | Supported  | Supported     | Supported      |
| Legacy Eval Mode | Supported  | Not supported | Not supported  |

A green check mark in the table means that the function can be called from that runtime, while a red cross means that calling the function from that runtime will throw an error. So in this case, `scheduleOnUI` can be called from any runtime when Bundle Mode is on, but only from the RN Runtime when Bundle Mode is off:

The following example runs the same code in both modes: the RN Runtime schedules a worker, and that worker tries to schedule a function on the UI Runtime.

Legacy Eval Mode

The worker starts, but its call to `scheduleOnUI` throws. The UI function never runs.

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function showResult() {
  'worklet';
  console.log('UI received the result');
}

function sendResult() {
  'worklet';
  console.log('Worker is running');
  // Calling scheduleOnUI from a Worklet Runtime requires Bundle Mode.
  scheduleOnUI(showResult);
}

const worker = createWorkletRuntime({ name: 'background' });
scheduleOnRuntime(worker, sendResult);
```

Bundle Mode

The worker can call `scheduleOnUI`, so the UI Runtime receives the task and logs the result.

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function showResult() {
  'worklet';
  console.log('UI received the result');
}

function sendResult() {
  'worklet';
  console.log('Worker is running');
  // Calling scheduleOnUI from a Worklet Runtime requires Bundle Mode.
  scheduleOnUI(showResult);
}

const worker = createWorkletRuntime({ name: 'background' });
scheduleOnRuntime(worker, sendResult);
```

# Compatibility table

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/compatibility

# Compatibility table

> INFO
>
> The Worklets library isn't tested on the Legacy Architecture (Paper). We highly recommend migrating to the New Architecture (Fabric) prior to using the Worklets library.

**The table assumes you're using the latest patch of each minor version of the Worklets library.**
For example, `0.7.x` shows support for React Native `0.84` because Worklets `0.7.4` added it, even though `0.7.0` didn't have it. If you're on an older patch, check the `compatibility.json` file in the Worklets package for exact version support.

### Supported React Native versions

The rule of thumb is that the Worklets library supports at least the last three minor versions of React Native.

---

# Feature flags

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/feature-flags

# Feature flags

Feature flags allow developers to opt-in for experimental changes or opt-out from recent changes that have already been made default. Feature flags serve as a tool for incremental rollout of new implementation without affecting the general stability of the library, allowing to gather feedback from early adopters. There are two types of feature flags: static and dynamic.

## Summary of available feature flags

| Feature flag name                                                                                                                                              |                                                         Type                                                         | Added in | Removed in | Default value |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------: | :------: | :--------: | :-----------: |
| [`IOS_DYNAMIC_FRAMERATE_ENABLED`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/feature-flags#ios_dynamic_framerate_enabled)         | [static](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/feature-flags#static-feature-flags) |   0.6.0  |      –     |     `true`    |
| [`FETCH_PREVIEW_ENABLED`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/feature-flags#fetch_preview_enabled)                         | [static](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/feature-flags#static-feature-flags) |   0.8.0  |   0.13.0   |    `false`    |
| [`ENABLE_CROSS_RUNTIME_STACK_TRACES`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/feature-flags#enable_cross_runtime_stack_traces) | [static](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/feature-flags#static-feature-flags) |   0.9.0  |      –     |     `true`    |

> INFO
>
> Feature flags available in `react-native-reanimated` are listed [on this page](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-reanimated/docs/guides/feature-flags).

## Description of available feature flags

### `IOS_DYNAMIC_FRAMERATE_ENABLED`

This feature flags is supposed to improve the visual perception and perceived smoothness of computationally expensive animations. When enabled, the frame rate will be automatically adjusted for current workload of the UI thread. For instance, if the device fails to run animations in 120 fps which would usually results in irregular frame drops, the mechanism will fallback to stable 60 fps. For more details, see [PR #7624](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/pull/7624).

### `FETCH_PREVIEW_ENABLED`

**Removed in 0.13.0.** The [networking API on Worklet Runtimes](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode/usage#running-network-requests-in-worklets) is enabled by default in [Bundle Mode](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode) and no longer requires a feature flag. To leave it out of a particular runtime, pass [`enableNetworking: false`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/createWorkletRuntime#enablenetworking) to `createWorkletRuntime`.

### `ENABLE_CROSS_RUNTIME_STACK_TRACES`

When enabled, the JavaScript call site that schedules a worklet function (via `scheduleOnUI`, `scheduleOnRuntime` and similar) is captured and attached to the worklet function. If the worklet function then throws on the worklet runtime, the resulting error stack is stitched together with the original scheduling stack so the LogBox entry points back to the line that scheduled it, rather than ending at the worklet runtime boundary. This makes errors thrown deep inside worklet functions much easier to trace back to their origin in your app code.

This flag only takes effect in development builds (`__DEV__`). In release builds, capturing the scheduling stack is skipped regardless of the flag value to avoid the runtime overhead.

**Capturing extra stack trace data can significantly hurt performance in code paths that perform many async/worklet scheduling calls. We recommend opting out of this flag in those situations.**

Given the following snippet:

```tsx
import { scheduleOnUI } from 'react-native-worklets';

function hardToDebug(callback: () => void) {
  'worklet';
  callback();
}

function functionThatThrows() {
  'worklet';
  throw new Error("I'm not!");
}

function functionThatDoesntThrow() {
  'worklet';
  console.log("I'm okay");
}

export default function App() {
  // Which invocation throws?
  scheduleOnUI(hardToDebug, functionThatDoesntThrow);
  scheduleOnUI(hardToDebug, functionThatThrows);
  scheduleOnUI(hardToDebug, functionThatDoesntThrow);
  return null;
}
```

The call stack reported in LogBox differs depending on whether the flag is enabled:

**Enabled**

![Cross-runtime stack trace with flag enabled](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/img/cross-runtime-stack-trace-enabled.png)

**Disabled**

![Cross-runtime stack trace with flag disabled](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/img/cross-runtime-stack-trace-disabled.png)

The frames without the `[UI]:` prefix (`enqueueUI`, `scheduleOnUI`, `App`, ...) are the ones contributed by this feature. They come from the RN runtime call site that scheduled the worklet function. Without the flag, the stack stops at the worklet runtime boundary and only the `[UI]:` frames are visible.

## Static feature flags

Static flags are intended to be resolved during code compilation and cannot be changed during application runtime. To enable a static feature flag, you need to:

1. Add the following lines to `package.json` of your app

```json
{
  // ...
  "worklets": {
    "staticFeatureFlags": {
      "EXAMPLE_STATIC_FLAG": true
    }
  }
}
```

2. Run `pod install` (iOS only)
3. Rebuild the native app

> WARNING
>
> Static feature flags are not supported in environments where the Worklets library is prebuilt with the default configuration of flags, like for instance in [Expo Go](https://expo.dev/go) and [RNRepo](https://rnrepo.org/).
>
> * It's not possible to modify static feature flags in Expo Go. Please consider using [Expo Prebuild](https://docs.expo.dev/workflow/continuous-native-generation/) instead.
> * If your project uses RNRepo, you need to force building the Worklets library from source by adding it to the deny list as described in [RNRepo's documentation](https://github.com/software-mansion/rnrepo/blob/main/TROUBLESHOOTING.md#deny-list-configuration).

To read a static feature flag value in JavaScript, you can use `getStaticFeatureFlag` function.

## Dynamic feature flags

Dynamic flags can be modified during runtime and their values can change at any moment of app lifetime. To enable or disable a dynamic feature flag, you need to call `setDynamicFeatureFlag` function.

```tsx
import { setDynamicFeatureFlag } from 'react-native-worklets';

setDynamicFeatureFlag('EXAMPLE_DYNAMIC_FLAG', true);
```

To read a dynamic feature flag value in JavaScript, you can use `getDynamicFeatureFlag` function.

## Comparison of static and dynamic feature flags

|                                             | Static feature flags | Dynamic feature flags |
| ------------------------------------------- | :------------------: | :-------------------: |
| Value is known during app build             |           ✅          |           ❌           |
| Value may change during app lifetime        |           ❌          |           ✅           |
| Value change requires app rebuild           |           ✅          |           ❌           |
| Can be changed via public JavaScript API    |           ❌          |           ✅           |
| Can be changed via app's `package.json`     |           ✅          |           ❌           |
| Can be changed when using Expo Go or RNRepo |           ❌          |           ✅           |

## Remarks for contributors

* Feature flags should switch the implementation to the new experimental behavior only when enabled.
* Initially, the default value should be false, allowing users to opt-in for the experimental behavior when desired.
* When the experimental behavior is considered stable, the default value should be set to true, while still allowing users to opt-out if needed.
* After some period, the feature flag which is enabled by default should be removed from the codebase.
* Both static and dynamic feature flags should follow upper snake case, i.e. `EXAMPLE_FEATURE_FLAG`.
* The name of the feature flag should not contain the expression `FEATURE_FLAG` itself.
* It is recommended to explicitly use `ENABLE_` or `DISABLE_` prefix for feature flags that enable or disable certain parts of the code for the sake of clarity.

---

# Running worklet functions on the UI runtime

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/running-on-the-ui-runtime

# Running worklet functions on the UI runtime

The Worklets library provides three functions for running a [worklet function](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/concurrency-model#worklet-functions) on the [UI Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#ui-runtime) from the [RN Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#rn-runtime): [`scheduleOnUI`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnUI), [`runOnUIAsync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnUIAsync) and [`runOnUISync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnUISync).
They differ in whether the worklet function runs asynchronously or synchronously, and in what they return to the caller.
Use the table below to pick the one that fits your case.

## Comparison

|                 | [`scheduleOnUI`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnUI) | [`runOnUIAsync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnUIAsync) | [`runOnUISync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnUISync) |
| --------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Execution**   | Asynchronous                                                                                              | Asynchronous                                                                                              | Synchronous, blocks the caller until the worklet function returns                                       |
| **Returns**     | Nothing                                                                                                   | A `Promise` that resolves with the worklet function's return value                                        | The worklet function's return value directly                                                            |
| **Web support** | ✅                                                                                                         | ✅                                                                                                         | ❌                                                                                                       |
| **Use when**    | You want to run a worklet function on the UI Runtime and don't need its result back                       | You need the worklet function's result back, but don't want to block the calling thread                   | You need the worklet function's result immediately, within the same synchronous flow                    |

The values returned by `runOnUIAsync` and `runOnUISync` have to be [serializable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/serializable).

All three functions can be called from the [RN Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#rn-runtime), and additionally from the [UI](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#ui-runtime) and [Worker](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#worker-runtime) Runtimes when [Bundle Mode](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode) is enabled.
See [Call tables](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/call-tables) for the full matrix.

## Watch the execution

### Schedule work without waiting

The UI thread runs the callback while the JS thread continues with the next line.

```js
import { scheduleOnUI } from 'react-native-worklets';

function myFunction() {
  'worklet';
  console.log('Hello from the UI Runtime!');
}

scheduleOnUI(myFunction);
console.log('The RN Runtime continues');
```

### Await a result

The callback runs on the UI thread. Awaiting its Promise suspends this function; the JS thread remains available for other queued work.

```js
import { runOnUIAsync } from 'react-native-worklets';

function compute() {
  'worklet';
  return 1;
}

const pending = runOnUIAsync(compute);
console.log('The RN Runtime continues while the result is pending');
const result = await pending;
console.log(result); // 1
```

### Read a result synchronously

The calling JS thread acquires the UI Runtime and executes the callback itself. It resumes the next line only after the result is ready.

```js
import { runOnUISync } from 'react-native-worklets';

function myFunction(num) {
  'worklet';
  return num + 1;
}

const result = runOnUISync(myFunction, 0);
console.log(result); // 1
```

# Testing with Jest

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/guides/testing

# Testing with Jest

React Native Worklets is primarily a native library, for that reason it requires a proper setup to be tested with Jest. This guide will show you how to set it up when testing in a React Native project.

You have two options for this:

1. **Enforce the use of mock implementation for React Native Worklets.**

   React Native Worklets provides a complete mock implementation for Jest. This is the recommended approach for testing.

2. **Enforce the use of Web implementation for React Native Worklets.**

   React Native Worklets has a separate Web implementation to use in the browser. Use this approach when you want to avoid using artifical mocks.

## Using the mock implementation

Depending on whether you are using TypeScript or JavaScript, apply the following mock:

TypeScript

```js
jest.mock('react-native-worklets', () =>
  require('react-native-worklets/src/mock')
);
```

JavaScript

```js
jest.mock('react-native-worklets', () =>
  require('react-native-worklets/lib/module/mock')
);
```

## Using the Web implementation

Override Jest resolver to enforce resolving web implementation of React Native Worklets instead of pulling the native one. Modify your `jest.config.js` file to include the following code:

```js
module.exports = {
  // ... other configurations
  resolver: 'react-native-worklets/jest/resolver',
};
```
