# Concurrency model

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/concurrency-model

# Concurrency model

To understand the concurrency model of the Worklets library and why it's needed, we have to look at
how a React Native app is structured.

## The React Native model

A React Native app is, first and foremost, **a native app**. Like every native app, it has a main
thread — usually called the **User Interface (UI) thread** — that receives touches, lays out views
and draws them on screen.

Your JavaScript doesn't run there. At startup, the native app creates two things: a separate thread, the **JavaScript thread** (JS thread), and a [Hermes](https://reactnative.dev/docs/hermes) JavaScript
Virtual Machine (JSVM), also called a **JavaScript Runtime**. We'll call this Runtime the
[React Native Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#rn-runtime). Then, it delegates the execution of your JavaScript Bundle and its [event loop](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Execution_model#agent_execution_model) to the JS thread.

The JS thread executes all of your app's JavaScript code — your React components, your business
logic, your event handlers. Its job is to figure out what the screen should look like and tell the
UI thread how to render it.

This split is what the official docs call the
[threading model](https://reactnative.dev/architecture/threading-model).

> NOTE
>
> **A JavaScript Runtime and a thread aren't the same thing!**
>
> * **A JavaScript Runtime is an execution environment**: a set of native functions (CPU instructions)
>   to evaluate JavaScript code and data structures to store global objects, allocated JavaScript
>   values, and the current execution state.
>
> * **A thread is an OS-level primitive for executing CPU instructions.** The operating system decides
>   when and on which CPU core to run the thread.
>
> A JavaScript Runtime is an exclusive resource. A thread must acquire it before using it to execute
> JavaScript code. After the thread finishes execution and releases it, another thread can acquire it.

## Limitations

Since all your app logic lives inside the JavaScript Bundle and is executed only on one thread, you
might run into a situation where a critical UI event has to wait for the JS thread to trigger the respective JavaScript event handler, which makes the app visibly lag.

A similar situation happens if animation calculations are done with `useState` (please don't do this in real apps!) on a busy JS thread:

## Overcoming limitations

To solve this issue, we have to somehow move the execution of the UI-critical parts of our app off
the JS thread. We can't use a
[native module](https://reactnative.dev/docs/turbo-native-modules-introduction) if we want to keep
our logic
purely in JavaScript code. We can't forcefully run some JavaScript code on the UI thread
concurrently with the RN Runtime. JavaScript Runtimes are single-threaded by design, and doing so would result in an immediate crash.

This means that we have to create a new Runtime and move the event and animation logic outside the
RN Runtime to the new Runtime.

Now, when the event comes, we can synchronously handle it on the UI thread, using our new Runtime.
This is exactly the [UI Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#ui-runtime) that the Worklets library
exposes.

Moreover, we can also offload the heavy computation that kept our JS thread overloaded. It's better
not to delegate that work to the UI thread as it would make the app unresponsive. We don't want to
preempt the UI Runtime from another thread either — that could block the UI thread from handling the
touch event, as it has to wait for the UI Runtime to be released.

What we can do is spawn *another Runtime and a thread*. We'll dedicate that thread to executing tasks using the new Runtime. We'll call this Runtime a Worker Runtime.

This is how the Worklets library allows you to overcome bottlenecks on the RN Runtime and the JS
thread, while keeping your app's logic strictly in JavaScript.

## Delegating JavaScript

There's one last bit of the puzzle missing — it's not that simple to just send some JavaScript
functions from one Runtime to be executed on another Runtime. The single-threaded design of
JavaScript Runtimes makes casual JavaScript functions closely tied to a given Runtime instance and not suitable for any kind of serialization. For that purpose, we need some special functions.

## Worklet functions

**A worklet function** (also called just **a worklet**) is a JavaScript function that can be safely
moved and dispatched across JavaScript Runtimes within a React Native app.

To turn a casual JavaScript function into a worklet function, all you need to do is add the **`'worklet'` directive** at the top of your function.

```javascript
function myWorklet() {
  'worklet';
  console.log('I can be safely sent to any Runtime!');
}
```

Functions marked with the directive are transformed with the
[Worklets plugin](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/about), in a process we call **workletization**,
into special entities
that are safe to be juggled between JavaScript Runtimes.

It's time to learn how to use these worklet functions — in the next chapter.

---

# Returning results

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/returning-results

# Returning results

In the [previous chapter](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/your-first-worklet) we dispatched some console logs to
other Runtimes. However, logging itself is not particularly useful.

In this chapter we'll learn how to obtain execution results from dispatched worklet functions.

## Synchronously

This is the simplest way of returning values. [`runOnUISync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnUISync) and
[`runOnRuntimeSync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnRuntimeSync) functions return the result of a worklet
function directly to the invoking Runtime:

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  runOnRuntimeSync,
  runOnUISync,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function foo() {
  return 42;
}

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();
const uiResult = runOnUISync(foo);
const workerResult = runOnRuntimeSync(worker, foo);
console.log(uiResult, workerResult);
```

However, dispatching this calculation synchronously doesn't free the calling thread. We could
also call `foo` directly on the RN Runtime:

```js
function foo() {
  return 42;
}

const result = foo();
console.log(result);
```

Both the function and its caller execute on the JS thread and the result is immediately available.
To let the calling thread do other work while a calculation runs on another thread, we need an
asynchronous call. We'll explore when synchronous calls are useful in future sections.

## Asynchronously

For asynchronous returns, e.g. results of complex calculations, you can use
[`runOnUIAsync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnUIAsync) and
[`runOnRuntimeAsync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnRuntimeAsync) functions. They return an awaitable
promise.

Remember that [`scheduleOnUI`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnUI) and
[`scheduleOnRuntime`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnRuntime) functions do not return a value.

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  getCurrentThreadId,
  runOnRuntimeAsync,
  runOnUIAsync,
} from 'react-native-worklets';
import { doImportantStuff } from './mocks';

function complexTask() {
  console.log(`computing on thread ${getCurrentThreadId()}`);
  const value = doImportantStuff();
  console.log('done');
  return value;
}

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();
const uiResult = runOnUIAsync(complexTask);
const result = runOnRuntimeAsync(worker, complexTask);
console.log('dispatched, RN Runtime keeps going');
const first = await uiResult;
const second = await result;
console.log(first, second);
```

The scheduling Runtime is free to keep executing JavaScript code until you await the returned
promise. In this example we dispatched the invocations of `complexTask` before awaiting, to execute them concurrently. While the RN Runtime awaits, its thread is free to run other tasks.

## With callbacks

Often, we'll want to return a value through a callback, e.g. to update our app's React state based on the result of a worklet function executed on another Worklet Runtime. You might be tempted to
write something like this:

```js
import { createWorkletRuntime, scheduleOnRuntime } from 'react-native-worklets';
import { useState } from 'react';
import { doImportantStuff } from './mocks';

function Component() {
  const [state, setState] = useState(0);
  const worker = createWorkletRuntime({ name: 'worker' });
  function task() {
    const result = doImportantStuff();
    setState(result); // This call crashes on the Worker Runtime.
  }
  scheduleOnRuntime(worker, task);
  return null;
}
```

The worker calculates `result`, but stops when it tries to call `setState(result)`.
The state setter belongs to the RN Runtime. Passing it to the Worker Runtime gives that Runtime a reference to the callback, not a function it can invoke directly.

The console shows the Worklets error format. The function and Runtime names in your app may differ.

We have to dispatch it back to the RN Runtime with the [`scheduleOnRN`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnRN) function.

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnRN,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
} from 'react-native-worklets';
import { doImportantStuff } from './mocks';

function setState(value) {
  console.log(`state = ${value}`);
}

function task() {
  const result = doImportantStuff();
  scheduleOnRN(setState, result);
}

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();
scheduleOnRuntime(worker, task);
```

Alternatively, you can use a promise and the `runOnRuntimeAsync` function:

```js
import { createWorkletRuntime, runOnRuntimeAsync } from 'react-native-worklets';
import { doImportantStuff } from './mocks';

function setState(value) {
  console.log(`state = ${value}`);
}

function task() {
  const result = doImportantStuff();
  return result;
}

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();
runOnRuntimeAsync(worker, task).then((result) => setState(result));
```

Now that we know how to return values, in the next chapter we'll learn how to use a Worklet Runtime's event loop.

---

# Synchronizing data

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/synchronizing-data

# Synchronizing data

In the [previous chapter](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/using-event-loop) we learned some theory about event
loops.

In this chapter, we'll put it to use and explore more advanced patterns of synchronizing data between JavaScript Runtimes,
where [asynchronous returns we learned previously](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/returning-results) wouldn't be sufficient.

## Getting the result of a periodic task

Previous examples showed us how to return the result of a single worklet function call at the point of
its invocation. What if we had a long-running task, yielding results continuously, but we wanted to
poll the data only occasionally?

```js
import { createWorkletRuntime, scheduleOnRuntime } from 'react-native-worklets';

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();

function taskDispatch() {
  let result = -1;
  function task() {
    result++;
  }
  setInterval(task, 16);
}

scheduleOnRuntime(worker, taskDispatch);
// How to access `result` here?
```

We'll explore how we can obtain the value of the local `result` variable and pass it to the RN Runtime.

## With callbacks — anti-pattern

We could use the same pattern as
[returning results with a callback](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/returning-results#with-callbacks).

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnRN,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();

let polledResult = -1;
function pollResult(value) {
  polledResult = value;
}

function taskDispatch() {
  let result = -1;
  function task() {
    result++;
    scheduleOnRN(pollResult, result);
  }
  setInterval(task, 16);
}

scheduleOnRuntime(worker, taskDispatch);

function synchronize() {
  console.log(polledResult);
}

setInterval(synchronize, 80); // Only once in a while
```

**Do not do this!** This will schedule a cross-runtime call every 16 ms that updates our
`polledResult` value — even if we don't need it at the given moment. **For the best multithreading performance, minimize the number of cross-thread (cross-runtime) operations.**

## With the global object — anti-pattern

The simplest approach would be to store our result on the global object of the Worker Runtime.

Then poll it with another function call, either synchronously or asynchronously:

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  runOnRuntimeAsync,
  runOnRuntimeSync,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();

function taskDispatch() {
  globalThis.result = -1;
  function task() {
    globalThis.result++;
  }
  setInterval(task, 16);
}

scheduleOnRuntime(worker, taskDispatch);

function poll() {
  console.log('polling');
  return globalThis.result;
}
async function synchronize() {
  const asyncResult = runOnRuntimeAsync(worker, poll);
  const syncResult = runOnRuntimeSync(worker, poll);
  console.log('sync:', syncResult);
  const value = await asyncResult;
  console.log('async:', value);
}

setInterval(synchronize, 80); // Only once in a while
```

However, this code doesn't scale well if we want to synchronize with multiple variables. It's
generally a bad practice to use the global object like this. It's still better than the previous
anti-pattern, but please **use it as a last resort escape hatch.**

## With a Synchronizable

A [Synchronizable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/synchronizable) is a memory primitive in the Worklets library that lives outside of any Runtime's JavaScript heap. Reading it and writing to it doesn't require making a cross-runtime call and is the cheapest option for synchronizing data between Runtimes.

You can find detailed documentation for the Synchronizable in its
[API reference](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/synchronizable), but for the sake of this example we'll stick to its
`getDirty`
and `setBlocking` methods. The `getDirty` method simply returns the value of the Synchronizable, without
waiting for any
transactions on it to complete. It's safe to use it here as we don't care about reading the value
mid-transaction.
The `setBlocking` method updates the value atomically, blocking other writers from modifying it until
the transaction is complete.

```js
import {
  createSynchronizable,
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();
const result = createSynchronizable(-1);

function taskDispatch() {
  function task() {
    result.setBlocking((value) => value + 1);
  }
  setInterval(task, 16);
}

scheduleOnRuntime(worker, taskDispatch);

function synchronize() {
  console.log(result.getDirty());
}

setInterval(synchronize, 80); // Only once in a while
```

Even though the Synchronizable was created on the RN Runtime, the value actually lives in the native
heap and both Runtimes (threads) can access it with little overhead and without excessively blocking one
another.

For this simple case, we can even optimize our code further and use a
[Synchronizable with a fixed type](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/synchronizable#synchronizable-fixed),
which exposes the `setDirty` method and is generally faster than a general
[Synchronizable with a dynamic type](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/synchronizable#synchronizable-dynamic)
that we just used. A fixed-type Synchronizable holds a raw value instead of a general [Serializable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/serializable) on the native heap.

```js
import {
  createSynchronizable,
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();
const result = createSynchronizable(-1, { fixedType: true });

function taskDispatch() {
  let localResult = result.getDirty();
  function task() {
    localResult++;
    result.setDirty(localResult);
  }
  setInterval(task, 16);
}

scheduleOnRuntime(worker, taskDispatch);

function synchronize() {
  console.log(result.getDirty());
}

setInterval(synchronize, 80); // Only once in a while
```

This approach works best when you poll the data frequently or from multiple Runtimes at once.

The downside is that every call of `setDirty` or `setBlocking` has to cross the JavaScript–native boundary and store the value there. This is particularly costly when it comes to
storing non-primitive types, like objects or arrays, which require
[serialization](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/serializable)
on each boundary crossing.

## With a Shareable

A [Shareable](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/shareable) is another memory primitive, but, contrary to the Synchronizable, it lives on a designated Runtime, called the Host Runtime. Reading it on other Runtimes, called
Guest Runtimes,
means accessing it on its Host Runtime, either synchronously or asynchronously. It's similar in
principle to the [global object approach](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/synchronizing-data#with-the-global-object--anti-pattern), but with a layer
of useful
encapsulation.

Shareable is an *asymmetric* type, meaning it has a different structure on the Host Runtime and on
Guest Runtimes. On the Host Runtime, you can access the value it holds directly as its `value`
property. On Guest Runtimes you must use its synchronous or asynchronous methods.

To create a Shareable, we have to explicitly state the Host Runtime by its
[Runtime ID](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#worklet-runtime).

```js
import {
  createShareable,
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();
const initialValue = -1;
const result = createShareable(worker.runtimeId, initialValue);

function taskDispatch() {
  function task() {
    result.value++;
  }
  setInterval(task, 16);
}

scheduleOnRuntime(worker, taskDispatch);

async function synchronize() {
  const syncResult = result.getSync();
  const asyncResult = result.getAsync();
  console.log('sync:', syncResult);
  const value = await asyncResult;
  console.log('async:', value);
}

setInterval(synchronize, 80); // Only once in a while
```

This approach works best when the Host Runtime reads and updates the value often and Guest Runtimes read it only once in a while.

## Mixing Shareables with Synchronizables

Shareables and Synchronizables are a powerful combination. A Synchronizable can keep
information about
the state of the Shareable, i.e. whether it has been updated, so the Guest Runtime can avoid reading
it if it
hasn't changed.

This is how [Reanimated Shared Values](https://docs.swmansion.com/reanimated/docs/shared-values) are
implemented.

A Shareable hosted on the UI Runtime stores the animation progress. When the RN
Runtime wants
to read the value to synchronize with the UI — e.g. for a component's first render — it checks a
Synchronizable flag, `needsSync`, attached to the Shared Value, to see if the UI Runtime has updated the value. If not,
it returns the last
read value, which was cached locally on the RN Runtime.

If the value has been updated — the `needsSync` flag is set — only then does the RN Runtime synchronously preempt the UI Runtime from the UI thread to read the value directly from the Host
Runtime. This whole flow is visualized by the simulation below.

```js
import {
  UIRuntimeId,
  createShareable,
  createSynchronizable,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

const progress = createShareable(UIRuntimeId, 0);
const needsSync = createSynchronizable(false, { fixedType: true });
let cached = 0;

function onFrame(frame) {
  progress.value = frame * 25;
  needsSync.setDirty(true);
  if (frame < 4) {
    requestAnimationFrame(() => onFrame(frame + 1));
  }
}

function restartAnimation() {
  scheduleOnUI(onFrame, 0);
}

function refresh() {
  cached = progress.getSync();
  needsSync.setDirty(false);
  return cached;
}

function synchronize() {
  const changed = needsSync.getDirty();
  const value = changed ? refresh() : cached;
  console.log(`progress ${value}%${changed ? '' : ' (cached)'}`);
}

restartAnimation();
setInterval(restartAnimation, 160);
setInterval(synchronize, 24); // Read the progress on the RN Runtime once in a while
```

You might've noticed that the RN Runtime can read the `needsSync` flag in the tiny window when the UI Runtime has already updated the Shareable value but not yet the flag, so it reuses its cached result (lines 6-7 and 24-25). This is intended, as that example didn't aim for perfect synchronization.

If you want to avoid such tiny data races, you can lock the Synchronizable and perform a transaction instead. Do it only when you have to, as locking the Synchronizable like this is much more expensive than a plain `setDirty` call.

```js
import {
  UIRuntimeId,
  createShareable,
  createSynchronizable,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

const progress = createShareable(UIRuntimeId, 0);
const needsSync = createSynchronizable(false, { fixedType: true });
let cached = 0;

function onFrame(frame) {
  needsSync.lock(); // lock for transaction
  progress.value = frame * 25;
  needsSync.setDirty(true);
  needsSync.unlock(); // unlock
  if (frame < 4) {
    requestAnimationFrame(() => onFrame(frame + 1));
  }
}

function restartAnimation() {
  scheduleOnUI(onFrame, 0);
}

function refresh() {
  needsSync.setBlocking(false);
  cached = progress.getSync();
  return cached;
}

function synchronize() {
  const changed = needsSync.getBlocking();
  const value = changed ? refresh() : cached;
  console.log(`progress ${value}%${changed ? '' : ' (cached)'}`);
}

restartAnimation();
setInterval(restartAnimation, 160);
setInterval(synchronize, 24); // Read the progress on the RN Runtime once in a while
```

Note that we also had to change the `getDirty` call in the `synchronize` function to `getBlocking` — otherwise we wouldn't respect the lock and could still read the intermediate value.

In a future tutorial, we'll learn how to integrate the Worklets library with C++ code.

---

# Using the event loop

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/using-event-loop

# Using the event loop

In the [previous chapter](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/returning-results) we learned how to return results from
dispatched worklet functions.

In this chapter we'll learn some theory about event loops, which you can use for more robust
applications of worklet functions.

## Event loops in React Native

The event loops in React Native are similar to the ones
[in the browser](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Execution_model).
All event loop functions, like `setTimeout` or `requestAnimationFrame`, are available on the
[RN Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#rn-runtime) and on
[Worklet Runtimes](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#worklet-runtime), but they can behave slightly
differently depending on the context.

## RN Runtime

The RN Runtime's event loop is handled solely by the
[RN JS thread](https://reactnative.dev/architecture/threading-model). This means that, unlike in the browser, this Runtime's event loop *is not tied to the native rendering layer* and
[`requestAnimationFrame`](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Window/requestAnimationFrame) queue is polyfilled with a periodic timer.

However, the execution of the `requestAnimationFrame` queue is synced with the display's refresh rate, a technique known as [vertical synchronization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vertical_synchronization) (vsync). With an idle JS thread, the queue runs once per native frame.

This is the optimistic case. When the JS thread is busy, it cannot keep up and gets out of sync: it skips frames and then might flush the queue more often to catch up with the UI thread.

**The application UI will not wait for the current iteration of the RN Runtime's `requestAnimationFrame` queue
execution to finish when rendering a frame.**

In this recording, not only were there fewer JS thread frames than UI frames, but the RN Runtime counter on the screen also sometimes skipped a value — even though the timeline shows a separate queue execution for every value. The counter on the screen is drawn by the UI thread, after React Native has [committed and mounted](https://reactnative.dev/architecture/render-pipeline#phase-2-commit) the update. The UI thread draws only one frame per vsync. When the JS thread falls behind and then commits two updates within one frame, only the second one reaches the screen.

## UI Runtime

Unlike the RN Runtime, the UI Runtime's event loop is based entirely on the native rendering
layer. All operations scheduled with e.g. `requestAnimationFrame` or `setTimeout` will block the
native render until they finish.

With a busy JS thread, the UI Runtime still gets a `requestAnimationFrame` callback for every native
frame.

This implementation has trade-offs. Because the UI Runtime runs on the UI thread, its work might delay native rendering.

In the recording below, the UI Runtime does extra work in each frame, and the UI thread can't keep up with the vsync.
The JS thread is mostly idle, and the RN Runtime still executes its
`requestAnimationFrame` queue every vsync — but the UI can't render it in time anyway.

## UI Runtime timers

Timers like `setImmediate`, `setTimeout`, `setInterval` on the UI Runtime actually invoke
`requestAnimationFrame` under the hood. This means that, e.g., on a 60 Hz device, they run at most once
per 16 ms.

Here we call `requestAnimationFrame`, `setImmediate`, `setTimeout` and `requestAnimationFrame`
again on the UI Runtime. All four callbacks go to the same queue, so the `setImmediate` and
`setTimeout` callbacks run between the two `requestAnimationFrame` callbacks, in the next native frame.

```js
import { scheduleOnUI, setImmediate } from 'react-native-worklets';

function firstFrameCallback() {
  console.log('requestAnimationFrame 1');
}

function immediateCallback() {
  console.log('setImmediate');
}

function timeoutCallback() {
  console.log('setTimeout');
}

function secondFrameCallback() {
  console.log('requestAnimationFrame 2');
}

function scheduleCallbacks() {
  requestAnimationFrame(firstFrameCallback);
  setImmediate(immediateCallback);
  setTimeout(timeoutCallback, 0);
  requestAnimationFrame(secondFrameCallback);
}

scheduleOnUI(scheduleCallbacks);
```

## Worker Runtime

A Worker Runtime, which runs on its own dedicated thread, behaves similarly to the RN Runtime. Its
`requestAnimationFrame` queue is polyfilled with a periodic timer too.

Contrary to the RN Runtime, however, Worker Runtimes don't vsync their event loop queues by default. A `setInterval` with
a delay smaller than the vsync period might actually fire several times within a single native frame.

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function startTimer() {
  let count = 0;
  function tick() {
    count = count + 1;
    console.log('tick:', count);
    if (count === 4) {
      clearInterval(interval);
    }
  }
  const interval = setInterval(tick, 4);
}

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();
scheduleOnRuntime(worker, startTimer);
scheduleOnUI(startTimer);
startTimer();
```

For advanced use cases, you can create a Worker Runtime
[without the default event loop](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/createWorkletRuntime#enableeventloop) and then implement it
yourself.

In the next chapter we'll learn how to synchronize data between JavaScript Runtimes using the
available event loop APIs.

---

# Your first worklet function

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/your-first-worklet

# Your first worklet function

In this chapter we'll learn the basics of dispatching your JavaScript code to
[Worklet Runtimes](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#worklet-runtime) to execute in parallel, using
worklet
functions. We strongly recommend reading about the [concurrency model](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/tutorials/concurrency-model) before continuing.

## Creating a Worklet Runtime

To actually dispatch some multithreading work, we need another Worklet Runtime as a target. We can
either use the [UI Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#ui-runtime) which is always available,
or create our own [Worker Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#worker-runtime) with the [`createWorkletRuntime`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/createWorkletRuntime) function.

```js
import { createWorkletRuntime } from 'react-native-worklets';

const worker = createWorkletRuntime({ name: 'background' });
```

In the next steps we'll dispatch some work to our new Worker Runtime and the UI Runtime.

## Asynchronous execution

Let's start small by dispatching functions that perform only a `console.log` on different Runtimes. We'll print the TID (platform-specific thread id) of the executing thread too, to show
that they are indeed dispatched to different threads, with the [`getCurrentThreadId`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/getCurrentThreadId) function. This function returns the result
of [`std::this_thread::get_id`](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/thread/get_id).

We'll use [`scheduleOnUI`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnUI) to dispatch to the UI Runtime and
[`scheduleOnRuntime`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/scheduleOnRuntime) to dispatch to the Worker Runtime. These
functions are fire-and-forget style — they return immediately after dispatching the worklet
function, without waiting for it to complete, and do not yield any result.

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  getCurrentThreadId,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function logTid() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(getCurrentThreadId());
}

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();
logTid();
scheduleOnUI(logTid);
scheduleOnRuntime(worker, logTid);
```

The logs show a different TID for each call, because we dispatched the worklet function to different threads.

## Synchronous execution

Sometimes you might want to execute a worklet function synchronously, from the same thread, but on another Runtime. For that purpose, the Worklets library exposes
[`runOnUISync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnUISync) and
[`runOnRuntimeSync`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/runOnRuntimeSync) functions. These functions are blocking — they
return only after the worklet function has completed. If a different thread is currently using the Runtime, these functions wait for the target Runtime to be released before executing the worklet function.

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  getCurrentThreadId,
  runOnRuntimeSync,
  runOnUISync,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function logTid() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(getCurrentThreadId());
}

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();
logTid();
runOnUISync(logTid);
runOnRuntimeSync(worker, logTid);
```

All three logs show the same TID, because no thread hopping was involved.

Knowing when to delegate something asynchronously and when to do it synchronously is the difference
between a smooth user experience and a bad one. The rule of thumb is that **if the operation is not
critical for the UI, it should be dispatched asynchronously.**

## Passing arguments

If the worklet function you want to call takes arguments, you have to pass them as extra arguments to the scheduling function.

```js
import {
  createWorkletRuntime,
  getCurrentThreadId,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function logMessage(message) {
  'worklet';
  console.log(`${message} from thread ${getCurrentThreadId()}`);
}

const worker = createWorkletRuntime();
scheduleOnUI(logMessage, 'Hello');
scheduleOnRuntime(worker, logMessage, 'Hi');
```

## Autoworkletization

In previous code snippets we always marked worklet functions with the `'worklet'` directive.
However, in most cases you can omit the directive. The Worklets plugin
[automatically detects](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/about#autoworkletization) which functions should
be treated as worklet functions and applies the transformation regardless. Both versions below work
the same:

```js title="With the directive"
function logTid() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(getCurrentThreadId());
}

scheduleOnUI(logTid);
```

```js title="Without the directive"
function logTid() {
  console.log(getCurrentThreadId());
}

scheduleOnUI(logTid);
```

In future examples, we will omit the directive whenever possible.

In the next chapter, we'll learn how to return results from
worklet functions.

---

# getCurrentThreadId

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/getCurrentThreadId

# getCurrentThreadId

`getCurrentThreadId` returns the id of the thread which currently executes JavaScript on the calling [Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds). The returned id is a stringified result of [`std::this_thread::get_id()`](https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/thread/get_id).

## Reference

```js
import {
  getCurrentThreadId,
  runOnUISync,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function logThread() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(getCurrentThreadId());
}

logThread(); // The JS thread id.
scheduleOnUI(logThread); // The UI thread id.
runOnUISync(logThread); // The JS thread id.
```

Type definitions

```typescript
function getCurrentThreadId(): string;
```

### Returns

`getCurrentThreadId` returns a `string` with the id of the current thread. The format of the id is platform-specific.

## Call table

| Mode             | RN Runtime | UI Runtime | Worker Runtime |
| ---------------- | ---------- | ---------- | -------------- |
| Bundle Mode      | Supported  | Supported  | Supported      |
| Legacy Eval Mode | Supported  | Supported  | Supported      |

## Platform compatibility

| Native    | Web           |
| --------- | ------------- |
| Supported | Not supported |

---

# getRuntimeKind

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/getRuntimeKind

# getRuntimeKind

`getRuntimeKind` allows you to get the [kind of the current runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds). It's useful in advanced scenarios, where you need to check the runtime kind before executing certain code paths or where you need to have separate implementations per runtime.

`getRuntimeKind` is a direct replacement for the deprecated `_WORKLET` global variable.

We recommend using handy shorthands like [isRNRuntime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isRNRuntime), [isUIRuntime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isUIRuntime), [isWorkerRuntime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isWorkerRuntime), and [isWorkletRuntime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isWorkletRuntime).

## Reference

```js
import {
  getRuntimeKind,
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnUI,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function checkUI() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(getRuntimeKind()); // 2 (UI Runtime)
}

function checkWorker() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(getRuntimeKind()); // 3 (Worker Runtime)
}

console.log(getRuntimeKind()); // 1 (RN Runtime)
scheduleOnUI(checkUI);
const workerRuntime = createWorkletRuntime({ name: 'background' });
scheduleOnRuntime(workerRuntime, checkWorker);
```

Type definitions

```typescript
enum RuntimeKind {
  ReactNative = 1,
  UI = 2,
  Worker = 3,
}

function getRuntimeKind(): RuntimeKind;
```

### Returns

An enum value representing the current runtime kind:

* `1` for RN Runtime
* `2` for UI Runtime
* `3` for Worker Runtime

## Example

```typescript
import {
  getRuntimeKind,
  RuntimeKind,
  scheduleOnRN,
  scheduleOnUI,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function logToConsole(message: string) {
  console.log(message);
}

function log(message: string) {
  'worklet';
  if (getRuntimeKind() === RuntimeKind.ReactNative) {
    console.log(`RN: ${message}`);
  } else {
    // Fun fact - this is how `console.log` is implemented on Worklet Runtimes.
    scheduleOnRN(logToConsole, `UI: ${message}`);
  }
}

function randomDispatch() {
  if (Math.random() > 0.5) {
    scheduleOnUI(log, 'Hello!');
  } else {
    log('Hello!');
  }
}

randomDispatch(); // Could log either "RN: Hello!" or "UI: Hello!"
```

## Optimizations

For micro-optimizations of your code you can skip the invocation of `getRuntimeKind` and use the global variable `__RUNTIME_KIND` directly:

```typescript
console.log(globalThis.__RUNTIME_KIND); // 1 (RN Runtime)
```

Be aware that accessing the global variable `__RUNTIME_KIND` before importing anything from `react-native-worklets` might return `undefined` value. This is because the global variable is set only after the `react-native-worklets` module is loaded. This is especially important in Web contexts, where additional bundler optimizations may be in place.

## Remarks

* If you're using the global variable `__RUNTIME_KIND` make sure to reference it by accessing the global object, i.e. `globalThis.__RUNTIME_KIND` to avoid the pitfall where you accidentally reference a local variable with the same name.

---

# isBundleModeEnabled

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isBundleModeEnabled

# isBundleModeEnabled

Checks whether [Bundle Mode](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode) is enabled.

For instructions on how to enable Bundle Mode, see the [Bundle Mode documentation](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode).

## Reference

```typescript
import { isBundleModeEnabled } from 'react-native-worklets';

console.log(isBundleModeEnabled()); // true if Bundle Mode is enabled
```

Type definitions

```typescript
function isBundleModeEnabled(): boolean;
```

### Returns

`true` if Bundle Mode is enabled, `false` otherwise (including in [Legacy Eval Mode](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode#legacy-eval-mode) and on the Web).

---

# isRNRuntime

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isRNRuntime

# isRNRuntime

Checks if the current runtime is the [React Native Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#rn-runtime).

## Reference

```js
import {
  isRNRuntime,
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnUI,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function checkUI() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(isRNRuntime()); // false (UI Runtime)
}

function checkWorker() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(isRNRuntime()); // false (Worker Runtime)
}

console.log(isRNRuntime()); // true (RN Runtime)
scheduleOnUI(checkUI);
const workerRuntime = createWorkletRuntime({ name: 'background' });
scheduleOnRuntime(workerRuntime, checkWorker);
```

Type definitions

```typescript
function isRNRuntime(): boolean;
```

### Returns

`true` if the current runtime is the RN Runtime, `false` otherwise.

## Remarks

* The function checks the value of `globalThis.__RUNTIME_KIND` to determine the kind of the current runtime. See [getRuntimeKind](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/getRuntimeKind) for more details.

# isWorkletFunction

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isWorkletFunction

# isWorkletFunction

`isWorkletFunction` checks if a function is a worklet function. It only works with Worklets Babel plugin enabled. Unless you are doing something with internals of the Worklets library you shouldn't need to use this function.

## Reference

Both checks run on the RN Runtime. Checking a function doesn't execute it or schedule it on another thread.

```js
import { isWorkletFunction } from 'react-native-worklets';

function workletFunction() {
  'worklet';
  return 1;
}

function nonWorkletFunction() {
  return 1;
}

const isWorklet = isWorkletFunction(workletFunction);
console.log(isWorklet); // true

const isNonWorklet = isWorkletFunction(nonWorkletFunction);
console.log(isNonWorklet); // false
```

Type definitions

```typescript
type WorkletClosure = unknown[];

export type WorkletStackDetails = [
  error: Error,
  lineOffset: number,
  columnOffset: number,
];

interface WorkletInitData {
  /** Only when bytecode isn't toggled. */
  code?: string;
  /** Only in production builds and explicitly toggled. */
  bytecode?: ArrayBuffer;
  /** Only in dev builds. */
  location?: string;
  /** Only in dev builds. */
  sourceMap?: string;
}

interface WorkletProps {
  __closure?: WorkletClosure;
  __workletHash: number;
  /** Only in Legacy Eval Mode. */
  __initData?: WorkletInitData;
  /** `__stackDetails` is removed after parsing. */
  __stackDetails?: WorkletStackDetails;
  /** Only in dev builds. */
  __pluginVersion?: string;
}

type WorkletFunction<
  TArgs extends unknown[] = unknown[],
  TReturn = unknown,
> = ((...args: TArgs) => TReturn) & WorkletProps;

function isWorkletFunction<
  Args extends unknown[] = unknown[],
  ReturnValue = unknown,
>(value: unknown): value is WorkletFunction<Args, ReturnValue>;
```

### Arguments

#### value

A function to check if it is a worklet function.

### Returns

`isWorkletFunction` returns a boolean value.

### Remarks

* Do not call it before the worklet function is declared, as it will always return `false` then.

  ```ts
  isWorkletFunction(myWorklet); // Will always return false.

  function myWorklet() {
    'worklet';
  }
  ```

---

# isWorkletRuntime

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/utility/isWorkletRuntime

# isWorkletRuntime

Checks if the current runtime is a [Worklet Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#worklet-runtime), either the [UI Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#ui-runtime) or a [Worker Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#worker-runtime).

## Reference

```js
import {
  isWorkletRuntime,
  createWorkletRuntime,
  scheduleOnUI,
  scheduleOnRuntime,
} from 'react-native-worklets';

function checkUI() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(isWorkletRuntime()); // true (UI Runtime)
}

function checkWorker() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(isWorkletRuntime()); // true (Worker Runtime)
}

console.log(isWorkletRuntime()); // false (RN Runtime)
scheduleOnUI(checkUI);
const workerRuntime = createWorkletRuntime({ name: 'background' });
scheduleOnRuntime(workerRuntime, checkWorker);
```

Type definitions

```typescript
function isWorkletRuntime(): boolean;
```

`true` if the current runtime is a [Worklet Runtime](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#worklet-runtime), `false` otherwise.

## Remarks

# Worklets plugin

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/about

# Worklets plugin

## What is the Worklets plugin?

The Worklets plugin transforms your code so that it can run on the [Worklet Runtimes](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/runtimeKinds#worklet-runtime). It looks for functions marked with a `'worklet';` directive and converts them into serializable objects. We call this process [workletization](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/about#autoworkletization).

The Worklets plugin ships in two implementations. The Babel plugin (`react-native-worklets/plugin`) is the default. Starting from Worklets 0.13 you can also use the [Oxc plugin](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/oxc), a faster Rust port that supports [Bundle Mode](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode) only. Everything on this page applies to both.

* A function that contains a `'worklet'` directive at its very top, i.e.:

```ts
function foo() {
  'worklet';
  console.log('Hello from worklet');
}
```

* A function that is *autoworkletizable*, i.e.:

```ts
useAnimatedStyle(() => {
  // This function will run on the UI thread,
  // hence it's in a workletizable context and will be
  // autoworkletized. You don't need to add the 'worklet' directive here.
  return {
    width: 100,
  };
});
```

## What can be a worklet?

### JavaScript terms

The Worklets plugin supports the following terms as worklets:

#### Function Declarations

```ts
function foo() {
  'worklet';
  console.log('Hello from FunctionDeclaration');
}
```

#### Function Expressions

```ts
const foo = function () {
  'worklet';
  console.log('Hello from FunctionExpression');
};
```

#### Arrow Function Expressions

```ts
const foo = () => {
  'worklet';
  console.log('Hello from ArrowFunctionExpression');
};
```

#### Object Methods

```ts
const obj = {
  foo() {
    'worklet';
    console.log('Hello from ObjectMethod');
  },
};
```

### Class Methods

## Autoworkletization

To reduce boilerplate code and provide a safer API, the Worklets plugin detects automatically whether a function should be workletized. Thanks to that, you don't need to add the `'worklet'` directive to your callbacks:

```ts
import { scheduleOnUI } from 'react-native-worklets';

scheduleOnUI((greetings: string) => {
  // You don't need to add the 'worklet' directive here,
  // since plugin detects this callback as autoworkletizable.
  console.log(`${greetings} from UI Runtime`);
}, 'Hello');
```

This isn't limited to `scheduleOnUI` - the Worklets plugin autoworkletizes the callbacks that its APIs require to be worklet functions. This also covers callbacks in config objects, for example the `initializer` of [`createWorkletRuntime`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/threading/createWorkletRuntime). The plugin only checks specific argument positions and config keys, and a config object must be written inline in the call. The plugin also autoworkletizes some callbacks in [React Native Reanimated](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/blob/main/packages/react-native-worklets/plugin/src/layoutAnimationAutoworkletization.ts) and [React Native Gesture Handler](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/blob/main/packages/react-native-worklets/plugin/src/gestureHandlerAutoworkletization.ts). The whole list can be found in the [plugin source code](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/blob/main/packages/react-native-worklets/plugin/src/autoworkletization.ts).

Keep in mind that in more advanced use cases, you might still need to manually mark a function as a worklet function.

### Referencing worklet functions

You can define worklet functions **before** they are used and the plugin will autoworkletize them too:

```ts
function foo() {
  // You don't need to add
  // the 'worklet' directive here.
  return { width: 100 };
}

// You don't need to define an inline function here,
// a reference is enough.
const style = useAnimatedStyle(foo);
```

### Objects aggregating worklet functions

In some APIs, like `useAnimatedScrollHandler` you can pass an object that contains worklet functions instead of a function:

```ts
const handlerObject = {
  // You don't need to mark these methods as worklets.
  onBeginDrag() {
    console.log('Dragging...');
  },
  onScroll() {
    console.log('Scrolling...');
  },
};

const handler = useAnimatedScrollHandler(handlerObject);
```

### \[Experimental] Workletizing whole files

You can mark a file as a workletizable file by adding the `'worklet'` directive to the top of the file.

This will workletize all *top-level* [JavaScript terms](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/about#javascript-terms) automatically. It can come in handy for files that contain multiple worklet functions.

```ts
// file.ts
'worklet';

function foo() {
  // Function 'foo' will be autoworkletized.
  return { width: 100 };
}

function bar() {
  // Function 'bar' will be autoworkletized.
  function foobar() {
    // Function 'foobar' won't since it's not defined in top-level scope.
    console.log("I'm not a worklet");
  }
  return { width: 100 };
}
```

## Limits of autoworkletization

The plugin cannot infer whether a function is autoworkletizable or not in some contexts.

### Imports

When importing a function from another file or a module and using it as a worklet function, you must manually add the `'worklet'` directive to the function:

```ts
// foo.ts
import { bar } from './bar';
// ...
const style = useAnimatedStyle(bar);

// bar.ts
export function bar() {
  'worklet'; // Won't work without it.
  return {
    width: 100,
  };
}
```

### Custom hooks

Currently Worklets doesn't expose APIs that would allow you to register your custom hooks for callback workletization. This however, might change in the future.

### Expressions

A function won't get automatically workletized when it's a result of an expression. You have to add the `'worklet';` directive to make it work:

```ts
const foo = someCondition
  ? () => {
      'worklet'; // Won't work without it.
      return { width: 100 };
    }
  : () => {
      'worklet'; // Won't work without it.
      return { width: 200 };
    };

const style = useAnimatedStyle(foo);
```

In such cases we recommend either handling the conditional logic in the worklet function itself or refactoring your code to eliminate the need for conditional worklet functions.

## Pitfalls

There are some patterns that won't work with the plugin.

### Hoisting worklet functions

Worklet functions aren't hoisted. This means that you can't use worklet functions before they are defined:

```ts
// The following line crashes,
// even though 'foo' is marked as a worklet.
const style = useAnimatedStyle(foo);

function foo() {
  'worklet';
  return { width: 100 };
}
```

## Notes

If you feel like the Worklets plugin could make use of some new functionality or that its pitfalls are too severe, feel free to let us know on [GitHub](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/), via an issue or a discussion thread - and as always, PRs are welcome!

---

# Oxc plugin

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/oxc

# Oxc plugin

> NOTE
>
> The Oxc plugin is a port of the [Worklets Babel plugin](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/about) to Rust, built on top of [Oxc](https://oxc.rs/). It's an opt-in alternative to the Babel plugin, which remains the default for the time being. Only [Bundle Mode](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode) is supported.

## Setup

For setup instructions, refer to the [Bundle Mode setup](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode/setup?worklets-plugin=oxc#configure-worklets-plugin) with the Oxc plugin selected in the tabs.

## Options

The Oxc plugin accepts the [`importForwarding`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/plugin-options#importforwarding) option and it works the same way as in the Babel plugin.

[`bundleMode`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/plugin-options#bundlemode) and [`strictGlobal`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/plugin-options#strictglobal) are always on and cannot be turned off. The remaining options of the Babel plugin are ignored.

## Notes

Being a port, the Oxc plugin might not cover every edge case that the Babel plugin does. If you find a difference in behavior, please let us know on [GitHub](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/).

---

# Options

Source: https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/plugin-options

# Options for Worklets Babel Plugin

Our plugin offers several optional functionalities that you may need to employ advanced APIs:

Type definitions

```typescript
interface PluginOptions {
  bundleMode?: boolean;
  disableInlineStylesWarning?: boolean;
  disableSourceMaps?: boolean;
  disableWorkletClasses?: boolean;
  extraPlugins?: string[];
  extraPresets?: string[];
  getHBCBinary?: () => string;
  globals?: string[];
  hermesBytecode?: boolean;
  omitNativeOnlyData?: boolean;
  relativeSourceLocation?: boolean;
  strictGlobal?: boolean;
  substituteWebPlatformChecks?: boolean;
  importForwarding?: {
    moduleNames?: string[];
    relativePaths?: string[];
  };
}
```

## How to use

Using this is straightforward for Babel plugins; you just need to pass an object containing the options to the plugin in your `babel.config.js` file. Make sure to pass the plugin and its options as a **two-element array**.

Here's an example:

```js {13-16}
/** @type {import('react-native-worklets/plugin').PluginOptions} */
const workletsPluginOptions = {
  bundleMode: true,
  disableInlineStylesWarning: true,
  globals: ['myObjectOnUI'],
  substituteWebPlatformChecks: true,
}

module.exports = {
  ...
  plugins: [
    ...
    [
      'react-native-worklets/plugin',
      workletsPluginOptions
    ],
  ],
};
```

## Options

If you are using the Oxc plugin, refer to [Oxc plugin options](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/oxc#options).

### bundleMode

Defaults to `false`.

Enables the [Bundle Mode](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode).

### disableInlineStylesWarning

Defaults to `false`.

Turning on this option suppresses a helpful warning when you use [inline shared values](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-reanimated/docs/fundamentals/glossary#animations-in-inline-styling) and might unintentionally write:

```tsx
import Animated, {useSharedValue} from 'react-native-reanimated';

function MyView() {
  const width = useSharedValue(100);
  return <Animated.View style={{ width: width.value }}>; // Loss of reactivity when using `width.value` instead of `width`!
}
```

You'll receive a warning about accessing `value` in an inline prop and the potential loss of reactivity that it causes. However, because there's no fail-safe mechanism that checks if the accessed property `value` comes from a Shared Value during Babel transpilation, it might cause problems:

```tsx
import { View } from 'react-native';

interface MyProps {
  taggedWidth: {
    tag: string;
    value: number;
  };
}

function MyView({ taggedWidth }) {
  return <View style={{ width: taggedWidth.value }} />; // This triggers a false warning.
}
```

Enable this option to silence such false warnings.

### disableSourceMaps

Defaults to `false`.

This option turns off the source map generation for worklet functions. Mostly used for testing purposes.

### disableWorkletClasses

Defaults to `false`.

Disables [Worklet Classes
support](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/about#class-methods).
You might need to disable this feature when using [Custom
Serializables](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/memory/registerCustomSerializable).

### extraPlugins

Defaults to an empty array.

This is a list of Babel plugins that will be used when transforming worklet functions' code with Worklets Babel Plugin.

### extraPresets

Defaults to an empty array.

This is a list of Babel presets that will be used when transforming worklet functions' code with Worklets Babel Plugin.

### getHBCBinary

> CAUTION
>
> Experimental feature.

Defaults to `undefined`.

Returns the absolute path to the Hermes bytecode compiler (`hermesc`) binary.
This option is part of the experimental [`hermesBytecode`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/plugin-options#hermesbytecode)
feature and is required when it is enabled — the plugin invokes this binary to
compile each worklet function.

```js
/** @type {import('react-native-worklets/plugin').PluginOptions} */
const workletsPluginOptions = {
  hermesBytecode: true,
  getHBCBinary: () => {
    // Return the absolute path to the `hermesc` binary for the current host machine.
  },
};
```

Example implementation is available [here](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/blob/7881f20a6778d25055e9127efaae0139562fde40/apps/fabric-example/babel.config.js#L28).

### globals

Defaults to an empty array.

This is a list of identifiers (objects) that will not be copied to the UI thread if a worklet function requires them. For instance:

```tsx
const someReference = 5;
function foo() {
  'worklet';
  return someReference + 1;
}
```

In this example, `someReference` is not accessible on the UI thread. Consequently, we must copy it there, ensuring correct scoping, to keep the worklet function from failing. But, consider this:

```tsx
function bar() {
  'worklet';
  return null;
}
```

Here, the identifier `null` is already accessible on the UI thread. Therefore, we don't need to copy it and use a copied value there. While it might not immediately seem particularly useful to avoid copying the value, consider the following case:

```tsx
function setOnJS() {
  global.something = 'JS THREAD';
}

function setOnUI() {
  'worklet';
  global.something = 'UI THREAD';
}

function readFromJS() {
  console.log(global.something);
}

function readFromUI() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(global.something);
}

function run() {
  setOnJS();
  scheduleOnUI(setOnUI);
  readFromJS();
  scheduleOnUI(readFromUI);
}
```

Without `global` as a blocklisted identifier in this case, you'd only get:

```
JS THREAD
JS THREAD
```

This output occurs because the entire `global` object (!) would be copied to the UI thread for it to be assigned by `setOnUI`. Then, `readOnUI` would again copy the `global` object and read from this copy.

There is a [huge list of identifiers blocklisted by default](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/blob/main/packages/react-native-worklets/plugin/src/globals.ts).

### hermesBytecode

> CAUTION
>
> Experimental feature.

Defaults to `false`.

Enabled compilation of worklet functions to [Hermes](https://github.com/facebook/hermes) bytecode
ahead of time instead of shipping them as source strings in [Legacy Eval Mode](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode#legacy-eval-mode).
At runtime the Worklet Runtime evaluates the precompiled bytecode directly,
skipping code evaluation overhead costs.

This is a workaround for the [increased memory consumption of `eval` calls
in Hermes](https://github.com/software-mansion/react-native-reanimated/issues/9650).

Enabling it requires the
[`getHBCBinary`](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/plugin-options#gethbcbinary) option so the plugin can locate the Hermes compiler.

Bytecode is only emitted for production builds.
This option has no effect in [Bundle Mode](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode).

### omitNativeOnlyData

Defaults to `false`.

This option comes in handy for Web apps. Because Babel ordinarily doesn't get information about the target platform, it includes worklet data in the bundle that only Native apps find relevant. If you enable this option, your bundle size will be smaller.

### relativeSourceLocation

Defaults to `false`.

This option dictates the passed file location for a worklet function's source map. If you enable this option, the file paths will be relative to `process.cwd` (the current directory where Babel executes). This can be handy for Jest test snapshots to ensure consistent results across machines.

### strictGlobal

> NOTE
>
> We highly recommend enabling this option as it will be enabled by default in the future.

Defaults to `false`.

This option changes how global variables are handled inside worklet functions. You can read more about closures and global scoping [here](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/concepts/closures#global-scoping).

With this option disabled, accessing global variables inside worklet functions will lead to capturing them from the scheduler scope:

```tsx
global.something = 10;

function setOnUI() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(something); // Captured from scheduler scope, prints 10
}
```

When you enable `strictGlobal`, accessing a global variable inside a worklet function will result in accessing it directly from the global scope of the worklet runtime:

```tsx
global.something = 10;

function setOnUI() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(something); // undefined - accessed from worklet global scope
}
```

To actually access the global variable from another runtime you must assign it to a local variable and use it in the worklet function:

```tsx
global.something = 10;
const localSomething = global.something;

function setOnUI() {
  'worklet';
  console.log(localSomething); // prints 10
}
```

While it might seem handy to copy everything implicitly, it can lead to unexpected behavior when the captured object shouldn't be copied between runtimes. Compare this to the [globals option](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/worklets-plugin/plugin-options#globals), which allows you to specify which global variables should not be copied to the worklet runtime at all.

`strictGlobal` takes precedence over the `globals` option.

### substituteWebPlatformChecks

Defaults to `false`.

This option can also be useful for Web apps. In Reanimated, there are numerous checks to determine the right function implementation for a specific target platform. Enabling this option changes all the checks that identify if the target is a Web app to `true`. This alteration can aid in tree-shaking and contribute to reducing the bundle size.

### importForwarding

Defaults to no forwarding (an empty object).

Configures [import forwarding](https://docs.swmansion.com/react-native-worklets/docs/unreleased/bundleMode/importForwarding) for Bundle
Mode. See the dedicated page for the full overview.

#### importForwarding.moduleNames

Defaults to an empty array.

List of exact module names that should be forwarded as imports inside worklet functions.

For example, to use all exports from `my-library` directly on the Worklet
Runtime, add it to the list:

```javascript
/** @type {import('react-native-worklets/plugin').PluginOptions} */
const workletsPluginOptions = {
  // ...
  importForwarding: { moduleNames: ['my-library'] },
};
```

At bundle time, when a worklet function imports from `my-library`, the plugin forwards
that import into the worklet body:

Before
After (conceptually)

The module name has to be an exact match — with `my-library` in the list, an
import from `my-library/some-file` won't be forwarded:

Before
After (conceptually)

#### importForwarding.relativePaths

Defaults to an empty array.

List of paths that determine whether a module should forward its **relative**
imports inside worklet functions. If a module's path matches any of the provided paths,
all relative imports inside that module's worklet functions will be forwarded.

Use this when authoring a library that calls helpers via relative imports
inside its own worklet functions:

```javascript title="my-library/index.js"
import { someExport } from './utils';

function foo() {
  'worklet';

  // We want it forwarded.
  someExport();
}
```

Add the library's path to `relativePaths`:

```javascript
/** @type {import('react-native-worklets/plugin').PluginOptions} */
const workletsPluginOptions = {
  // ...
  importForwarding: { relativePaths: ['my-library'] },
};
```

At bundle time, the plugin forwards relative imports inside `my-library` into
the worklet body:

Before
After (conceptually)

You can also narrow the path to a subdirectory — e.g. `my-library/src` or
`my-library/src/utils` — to forward imports from only part of the library.

`moduleNames` won't work here: adding `'./utils'` to it would forward every
`'./utils'` import across the bundle, potentially breaking other libraries
with a file at the same relative path. `relativePaths` scopes forwarding to a
specific package.
